Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that weekly.
  • In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user indicates "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

In a recent development, then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

Industry observers note that the first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

In a recent development, the safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Sources indicate that here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

According to recent reports, nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = newly introduced LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

According to recent reports, you can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

It has been revealed that plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email reveals up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

Sources indicate that the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Industry observers note that free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Industry observers note that tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

It has been revealed that give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Industry observers note that limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

Sources indicate that A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = fresh RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

In a recent development, build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a upcoming case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every upcoming prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

  • It has been revealed that arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin has sued sweepstakes casino operator VGW and prediction market Kalshi on the same day, alleging illegal gambling under state law.

  • Both cases allege illegal gambling and violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin has sued sweepstakes casino operator VGW and prediction market Kalshi on the same day, alleging illegal gambling under state law. The VGW complaint puts a dollar figure on the state's sweepstakes market and adds Arkansas to a growing list of states challenging the dual-currency model.

Industry observers note that arkansas has opened a two-front legal fight against online gambling it says is unlicensed. One lawsuit targets VGW, the organization behind Chumba Casino, LuckyLand and Global Poker. The other targets KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc., the companies that own the Kalshi prediction market.

Both cases allege illegal gambling and violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Both also include an unjust enrichment claim. In each case the state seeks restitution, penalties, taxes and injunctive relief.

The VGW suit attacks the Gold Coin/Sweeps Coin model that almost every US sweepstakes casino relies on. It names ten affiliated VGW companies. The complaint indicates VGW reported about $66 million in taxable Arkansas sales between July 2025 and June 2026 and paid about $6 million in sales and use tax over that period, Gaming.net reported.

Those figures show a organization declaring sales to the state and paying tax on them. Yet VGW holds no Arkansas casino license, the state alleges. The complaint also accuses VGW of letting 18-year-olds play, even though Arkansas casinos require players to be 21.

The case lands less than two months after the New York settlement. New York Attorney General Letitia James confirmed that deal on September 9, 2026. It covered Chumba Casino, Global Poker and Luckyland Slots. VGW’s coin-based games were already off the table for New Yorkers by then, after her office sent the company a cease-and-desist letter in June 2025.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman went to court a few months earlier, claiming VGW’s sweepstakes casinos break Kentucky gambling law. Florida has also moved against dual-currency sweepstakes since June 2026. Arkansas now joins Kentucky, Florida and Upcoming York on that list. For operators using the same coin structure, the pattern points to rising legal exposure state by state.

The Kalshi complaint rests on a constitutional definition. The Arkansas Constitution’s definition of casino gaming expressly covers accepting wagers on sporting events. Kalshi has never held a casino-gaming license from the state commission, the state alleges. Nor has it held any other Arkansas authorization to take sports wagers.

It has been revealed that the complaint expressly limits itself to state-law claims and relief under Arkansas law. That choice means the state is relying on its own consumer-protection statute rather than waiting on the CFTC. Money lost, betting that gets out of hand, and depression or other damage to mental health are dangers Kalshi understands its customers face, Griffin’s office noted.

Today I filed a lawsuit against VGW, an online gaming platform that features such games as @ChumbaCasino, LuckyLand Casino, @LuckyLandSlots, and @official_glp.

It has been revealed that arkansas’s gambling laws are clear. If you’re providing a means for Arkansans to gamble money within our state, you are… pic.twitter.com/qs2dhRMC8K.

— Attorney General Tim Griffin (@AGTimGriffin) November 4, 2026.

Industry observers note that filing both cases on the same day signals how Arkansas views the two products. The attorney general is treating sweepstakes casinos and sports event contracts as the same kind of unlicensed gambling. Other states may weigh whether to copy that approach.

In a recent development, the VGW case was filed in White County Circuit Court. The Kalshi case was filed in Independence County Circuit Court.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another.
  • Recent findings suggest that holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

In a recent development, building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

Recent findings suggest that holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to update a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and company career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

According to recent reports, once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Recent findings suggest that computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop.

#57747. Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
  • I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
  • It has been revealed that the Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that notable to me day-to-day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

It has been revealed that the Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that notable to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

It has been revealed that my love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

Industry observers note that after a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

In a recent development, if you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

Recent findings suggest that I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

Recent findings suggest that I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this concern.

This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

Recent findings suggest that when the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Industry observers note that swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

Industry observers note that with audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

According to recent reports, this had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

Industry observers note that I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

It has been revealed that the experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that fanDuel's US adjusted EBITDA nearly disappeared in the third quarter of 2026, even as US revenue rose 6%.
  • In a recent development, fanDuel’s US business barely turned a profit in the third quarter of 2026.
  • For the regulated US market, the result reveals how much prediction-market spending is costing one of its online leaders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fanDuel's US adjusted EBITDA nearly disappeared in the third quarter of 2026, even as US revenue rose 6%. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its Alberta launch, while FanDuel Casino's revenue growth slowed to 8%.

In a recent development, fanDuel’s US business barely turned a profit in the third quarter of 2026. US adjusted EBITDA came in at just $3 million, against $51 million a year earlier. Revenue moved the other way, climbing 6% to $1.455 billion. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its launch in Alberta.

For the regulated US market, the result reveals how much prediction-market spending is costing one of its online leaders. The parent organization also lowered its full-year outlook for 2026. Buybacks are on hold for the foreseeable future so Flutter can focus on organic investment and paying down debt. Leverage stood at 4.6x at the end of the quarter, up from 3.7x in December 2025.

The group’s net loss widened to $1.148 billion from $789 million a year earlier. That figure includes impairments tied to Brazil, where Flutter stopped operating on Sept. 26, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that fanDuel Casino is adding players much faster than it is adding revenue. Flutter pointed to competition and to slower growth as US iGaming states mature. The contrast with late 2025 is sharp. In the fourth quarter of 2025, FanDuel Casino grew revenue 33% and held 28% of US iGaming gross gaming revenue.

Flutter put that share at 27% for the three months to Sept. 30, the same level it reported for the second quarter. An outside estimate is lower. FanDuel’s iGaming share was 25.1%, down from 26.6% a year earlier, according to Citizens figures published by NEXT.io. The same figures indicated US iGaming growth slowing to 12% year over year in the third quarter, the lowest on record.

Sportsbook revenue grew 4%. FanDuel’s share of US sportsbook gross gaming revenue slipped to 36%, from 39% in the second quarter. Its share of handle was 33%.

Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?
  • In a recent development, over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone tech giant.
  • The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

In a recent development, over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone tech giant. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

The answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

Sources indicate that ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

In a recent development, the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

Industry observers note that the main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

Recent findings suggest that the same issue cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

Sources indicate that portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens concern or some weird setting.

Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

In a recent development, overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

Latest Update: Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.
  • We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.
  • Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

Sources indicate that VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that this capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection.

Industry observers note that as shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

The SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function.

This capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

The OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

According to recent reports, the Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning).

In a recent development, capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above indicates a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:.

Industry observers note that multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Sources indicate that multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:.

The baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

Recent findings suggest that VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

In a recent development, the VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:.

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline.

Tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

Industry observers note that specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

Final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score.

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:.

Sources indicate that we now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

In a recent development, since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

Sources indicate that the instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis.

The Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth.

It has been revealed that multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid).

Recent findings suggest that the final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type.

Recent findings suggest that policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

Recent findings suggest that VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA indicates that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

Think your agent is solid? Put it to the test.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.

Breaking: Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.
  • Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.
  • According to recent reports, referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Play is introducing new adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

According to recent reports, referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or upgrade on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing new apps or updating your store listing.”.

Curious to see whether the requirements will actually be as strict as they make them seem (on paper).

If so, then also Google will have a ton of work to do to modernise all of their apps.

By August 2027, latest and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”.

Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”.

On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

Latest Update: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • In a recent development, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query.
  • According to recent reports, if you're new to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the latest multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

In a recent development, as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

According to recent reports, if you're new to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

General-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

Consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the tech giant's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

In a recent development, by finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:.

Sources indicate that the multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

It has been revealed that the most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

To finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):.

You can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:.

Industry observers note that in both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:.

Instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:.

Recent findings suggest that since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

This approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

According to recent reports, for this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:.

The train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:.

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:.

It has been revealed that the data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

In a recent development, for this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:.

More negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

In a recent development, the mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is key to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:.

In a recent development, to produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:.

This is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

In a recent development, the SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:.

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:.

To track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:.

Industry observers note that the evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory problems during evaluation of the large VLM.

Industry observers note that the SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:.

In a recent development, the training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:.

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

Sources indicate that after training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:.

The finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

The comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:.

Recent findings suggest that the finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most important information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

The gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report reveals two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Industry observers note that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

According to recent reports, A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

Recent findings suggest that this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

In a recent development, before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a upcoming purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

According to recent reports, for this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

In a recent development, keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

It has been revealed that campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

"utm_id", "utm_content", "utm_term".

const value = params.get(key)?.trim();.

return value && value.length <= 200.

Sources indicate that the browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Sources indicate that keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

It has been revealed that treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

According to recent reports, missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

In a recent development, caller ID is a separate matter. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

It has been revealed that A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",.

"data": { "status": "completed" }.

Sources indicate that the event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",.

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,.

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||.

throw upcoming TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");.

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {.

Sources indicate that contact_ref: input.contactRef ?? null,.

It has been revealed that attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,.

It has been revealed that resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

Recent findings suggest that for a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a latest one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

According to recent reports, twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Sources indicate that consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

Industry observers note that A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

In a recent development, here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),.

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,.

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),.

attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,.

UNIQUE (tenant_id, source, event_id),.

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id).

It has been revealed that the ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.
