💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.
  • While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.
  • This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.

While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.

This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.

By the end, you will have the same architecture used in this project: a background service worker that hosts models, a side panel chat UI, and a content script for page-level actions.

In this guide, we will recreate the core architecture of Transformers.js Gemma 4 Browser Assistant, using the published extension as a reference and the open-source codebase as the implementation map.

Recent findings suggest that before diving in, a quick scope note: I will not go deep on the React UI layer or Vite build configuration. The focus here is the high-level architecture decisions: what runs in each Chrome runtime and how those pieces are orchestrated.

If Manifest V3 is latest to you, read this short overview first: What is Manifest V3?.

In MV3, your architecture starts in public/manifest.json. This project defines three entry points:.

Sources indicate that the background service worker also handles chrome.action.onClicked to open the side panel for the active tab. Related entry point to know: a popup can be defined with action.default_popup and works well for quick actions. This project uses a side panel for persistent chat, but the orchestration pattern is the same.

The key design decision is to keep heavy orchestration in the background and keep UI/page logic thin.

One practical consequence of this division is that the conversation history also lives in background (Agent.chatMessages): the UI sends events like AGENT_GENERATE_TEXT, background appends the message, runs inference, then emits MESSAGES_UPDATE back to the side panel.

This split avoids duplicate model loads, keeps the UI responsive, and respects Chrome's security boundaries around DOM access.

In a recent development, once runtimes are separated, messaging becomes the backbone. In this project, all messages are typed through enums in src/shared/types.ts.

Industry observers note that creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you blueprint a production.

Image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

The ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

In a recent development, plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

It has been revealed that the key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

In a recent development, the right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the proposal you use.

Image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the tech giant’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

In a recent development, the pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

The quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

For the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

Industry observers note that A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

All third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

That makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

In the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

It has been revealed that the second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the firm’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

Sources indicate that bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active.
  • Focusing on long running agentic workloads.
  • This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

In a recent development, two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

It has been revealed that figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

In a recent development, heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

The layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

Industry observers note that efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a upcoming user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

According to recent reports, V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each upcoming user message.

V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

The schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

The agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

Three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

Industry observers note that the knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:.

Recent findings suggest that in the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% noted it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

According to recent reports, the long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Sources indicate that figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

Recent findings suggest that both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

The V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

It has been revealed that according to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

Tech Report: How to build scalable web apps with OpenAI's Privacy Filter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, openAI released Privacy Filter on the Hub this week: an open-source personally-identifiable information (PII) detector that labels text across eight categories in a single forward pass over a 128k context.
  • All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK.
  • Industry observers note that privacy Filter is a 1.5B-parameter model with 50M active parameters, permissively licensed under Apache 2.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI released Privacy Filter on the Hub this week: an open-source personally-identifiable information (PII) detector that labels text across eight categories in a single forward pass over a 128k context. Model card. We spent a few hours building with it and landed on three apps that each reveals a different slice of what it can do.

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

Industry observers note that privacy Filter is a 1.5B-parameter model with 50M active parameters, permissively licensed under Apache 2.0. PII categories are private_person, private_address, private_email, private_phone, private_url, private_date, account_number, secret. Context is 128,000 tokens. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PII-Masking-300k benchmark. Full numbers and methodology are in the official release blog.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

It has been revealed that user problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

What Privacy Filter does here. The whole file goes through in a single 128k-context forward pass, so there's no chunking, no stitching, and span offsets line up directly with the rendered text. BIOES decoding keeps span boundaries clean through long ambiguous runs.

What gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:.

It has been revealed that note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Image-Anonymizer.

It has been revealed that user problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

It has been revealed that what Privacy Filter does here. Tesseract runs OCR and returns per-word bounding boxes. The backend reconstructs the full text with a char-offset to box map, then runs Privacy Filter once over the whole text. Detected character spans are looked up against the word map and joined into pixel rectangles per line.

What gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:.

Industry observers note that the frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, new-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-SmartRedact-Paste.

Industry observers note that user problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

Sources indicate that what Privacy Filter does here. Swap each detected span with a placeholder on the stored paste. That's the entire redaction step. Multilingual text (Spanish, French, Chinese, Hindi, and others in the model-card examples) routes through the same call with no change.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :.

Industry observers note that A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:.

Sources indicate that @server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client owners hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

Drop in a resume, a screenshot of a Slack thread, a log line with a token in it. The fun part is seeing what Privacy Filter catches (and occasionally misses) on text you actually care about.

Nice demos — the 8-category Privacy Filter taxonomy is a strong EN consumer/sanitization baseline for pastebins and screenshots.

One gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Growth at MotorCity Casino outweighed declines at MGM Grand Detroit and Hollywood Casino at Greektown, lifting Detroit's October table and slot revenue from a year earlier. Retail sports betting also rebounded sharply from September, adding to the month's gains.

It has been revealed that motorCity Casino was the only Detroit property to grow table games and slot revenue in October from a year earlier. Its rivals both lost ground. MGM Grand Detroit slipped 2.7% to $51.3 million. Hollywood Casino at Greektown fell 5.0% to $21.6 million.

In a recent development, across the three casinos, tables and slots generated $108.1 million. That was up 2.1% from October 2025 and 5.2% from September 2026. Year-to-date revenue from January through October was up 2.3%.

CDC Gaming Reports put October 2025 table and slot revenue at $105.9 million.

MGM still holds the largest piece of the market. It took 47% of Detroit’s October revenue. MotorCity held 33%, and Hollywood Casino at Greektown held 20%.

Sources indicate that the October split continues a pattern from late summer. In August, MotorCity rose 8.3% to $33.8 million and MGM grew 2.3% to $52.9 million, while Greektown fell 2.6% to $22.2 million, InterGame reported. Detroit’s August total was $109.7 million.

Sources indicate that greektown’s slide deepened in September, when its revenue fell 8.8% year over year to $21.34 million. October’s decline was smaller. MGM, by contrast, moved from growth in August to a decline in October.

In a recent development, the citywide trend has been uneven. September table and slot revenue was 4.7% higher than a year earlier but 5.6% lower than in August. October’s rebound lifted aggregate revenue above September’s $103.55 million.

Sources indicate that retail sports betting produced $2.4 million in October. That compares with $769,771 in retail QAGR in September. Handle at the Detroit casinos was $12.87 million for the month.

Recent findings suggest that motorCity also led the sportsbook results. It posted $928,607 in retail receipts. MGM followed at $746,215, with Hollywood Casino at Greektown close behind at $729,350.

Industry observers note that the sportsbook activity generated $90,878 in state taxes. The casinos also sent $111,073 in sports wagering taxes to Detroit.

The city’s take from the casinos goes well beyond sports betting. In October, Detroit collected $13.4 million from the three properties, combining its share of gaming taxes with sums owed under each casino’s agreement with the city.

Benchmark highlightsBuilding on Nemotron Nano V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers substantial visual gains and adds entirely fresh audio and video+audio capabilities - while also leading another open-weights omni model, Qwen3-Omni, in many domains.

Recent findings suggest that efficiency highlightsCompared to other open omni models with the same interactivity, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers 7.4x higher system efficiency for multi-document use cases and 9.2x higher system efficiency for video use cases Figure 1. Total system throughput for multi-document and video use cases sustained by each model at a fixed per‑user interactivity threshold (tokens/sec/user).

At a high level, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is aimed at five classes of workloads:.

This is not only about OCR. The model is positioned for long, messy, high-value documents where understanding depends on layout, tables, figures, formulas, section structure, and cross-page references. Think contracts, technical papers, reports, manuals, multi-page forms, or compliance packets. The model can handle 100+ page documents.

According to recent reports, nemotron 3 Nano Omni includes strong speech understanding capabilities that enable high-quality transcription across diverse audio conditions. It handles long-form audio with varying speakers, accents, and background noise. These capabilities can be integrated into broader workflows, allowing spoken content to be transcribed, analyzed, and combined with other modalities for tasks like summarization, question answering, and cross-modal reasoning.

Many enterprise and developer workflows depend on mixed audio and visual evidence: screen recordings with narration, training videos, meetings with slides, tutorials, product demos, customer support captures, and long-form video archives. Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is built to reason over those inputs jointly.

The Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model is specifically trained for agentic computer use, enabling it to assist with tasks in graphical user interface (GUI) environments. Its capabilities include interpreting screenshots, monitoring the state of the user interface, grounding its reasoning in on-screen visuals, and helping with action selection or workflow automation.

It has been revealed that the model is designed for more than perception. It excels at reasoning-intensive tasks that require synthesizing information across long context windows, multiple modalities, and structured or semi-structured evidence. It can carry out multi-step reasoning, perform calculations, and connect signals from text, images, tables, and other inputs to arrive at coherent, well-supported answers.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a unified encoder-projector-decoder design. The language backbone is Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, paired with the C-RADIOv4-H vision encoder and the Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 audio encoder. The modality-specific encoders connect into the LLM backbone through lightweight projectors.

It has been revealed that figure 2. Model architecture of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B.

The model backbone interleaves three key components: 23 Mamba selective state-space layers for efficient long-context processing; 23 MoE layers with 128 experts, top-6 routing, and a shared expert for conditional capacity; and 6 grouped-query attention layers to preserve strong global interaction and expressivity.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni combines state-space models, attention, and MoE in a unified design that maintains strong reasoning performance while remaining practical for long, multimodal contexts.

In a recent development, on the vision side, the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni replaces the tiling strategy used in the v2 model with dynamic resolution processing at native aspect ratio. Each image can be represented using a variable number of 16 x 16 patches, with a minimum of 1,024 to a maximum of 13,312 visual patches per image. For square images, this is equivalent to 512 x 512 and 1840 x 1840, respectively.

That flexibility is critical for handling high-resolution, complex visual inputs such as OCR-heavy documents, financial tables, slides, research figures, screenshots, and GUI layouts—especially when both fine details and overall structure need to be understood together.

Recent findings suggest that for video, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a dedicated Conv3D tubelet embedding path. Instead of embedding each frame independently, every pair of consecutive frames is fused into a single "tubelet" before the ViT, halving the number of vision tokens the language model has to attend to. This allows us to either double the number of frames with the same token budget, or halve the number of tokens with the same number of frames.

EVS is an crucial feature, enabled during inference time, that drops redundant video tokens after the vision encoder. This reduces latency and improves throughput while maintaining accuracy. The first frame of the video is kept entirely, then for each subsequent frame, EVS keeps the “dynamic” tokens where the video is changing and drops the “static” ones where nothing has changed from the previous frame. We combine this with Conv3D to enable superior compression: Conv3D fuses tokens from pairs of frames into one, and then EVS prunes redundant static information.

The audio side is powered by Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2, connected to the backbone through its own 2-layer MLP projector. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz, and the model is trained with inputs up to 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), while the LLM max context length supports 5+ hours.

Industry observers note that this represents a shift from traditional VLM pipelines by enabling native audio processing within a shared multimodal sequence, allowing audio, visual, and text tokens to be jointly modeled. This is crucial for scenarios like narrated screen recordings, video Q&A where speech alters visual meaning, long-form instructional or meeting content, and tasks requiring temporally grounded multimodal reasoning.

Sources indicate that each encoder is connected to the LLM with a lightweight 2-layer MLP projector that maps encoder features into the shared embedding space. Once projected, vision, audio, and text tokens are interleaved and processed jointly.

This design keeps the overall system modular while still enabling genuine cross-modal reasoning inside the backbone itself.

The SFT stages are trained on NVIDIA H100, scaling from 32 to 128 nodes depending on the stage. The stack uses Megatron-LM, Transformer Engine, and Megatron Energon, with tensor parallelism, expert parallelism, sequence parallelism, context parallelism for the long context stages, online sequence packing, and selective activation recomputation.

Sources indicate that post-SFT reinforcement learning uses NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym with a Megatron backend. The RL infrastructure used a Ray-based distributed setup across B200 and H100 clusters, plus multimodal deduplication, so repeated rollouts do not multiply image, video, and audio memory.

We open-source substantial parts of our training code.

We introduce multi-environment text and omni training in Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. Our text RL training stage happens across diverse environments in Nemo-Gym, which evaluates the model’s ability to perform sequences of actions such as tool calling, writing code, and multi-part planning that satisfy the verifiable criteria.

It has been revealed that omni RL trains the model to reason across images, video, audio, and text within a unified framework, covering tasks from single-modality to fully multimodal scenarios. A diverse verifier suite evaluates outputs across formats like multiple-choice, math, GUI grounding, and ASR, while intentionally including unanswerable cases to teach the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient rather than hallucinate.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is trained on an enhanced dataset that emphasizes high-quality reasoning across multiple modalities. We significantly expand task coverage and introduce synthetic data for complex reasoning scenarios where public datasets are limited. To support this, we build task-specific, multi-stage pipelines for scalable synthetic data generation.

As one example, we generated approximately 11.4M synthetic QA pairs (~45B tokens) from a large corpus of real-world PDFs using NeMo Data Designer. This dataset is used to strengthen long-context document reasoning during post-training and delivers a 2.19× improvement in overall accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc.

According to recent reports, we detail the full pipeline evolution, including failure analysis and key lessons learned, in our Data Designer developer note. The note also includes nine runnable pipeline recipes that can serve as starting points for building your own document-understanding datasets.

Converting Markdown to PDF is easy until the document has real content: long code blocks, wide tables, images and non-Latin text are where most tools fall apart.

Pandoc with LaTeX is still the most powerful route, but it needs a large install and trips over Unicode and emoji unless you switch engines and fonts.

Browser-based approaches (print CSS, Chromium-powered converters, in-browser tools) avoid the install and give you HTML-quality rendering, as long as you control page breaks.

A handful of print CSS rules (@page, break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid) fix the majority of ugly PDFs, whichever tool you use.

Choose the tool by the document: a quick README export, a long technical report and a multilingual document each have a different best option.

Sources indicate that I write almost everything in Markdown: READMEs, release notes, client handovers, meeting notes. And at least once a week, someone asks for "the PDF version". Every time, the conversion looks fine on the first page and falls apart somewhere around page three: a code block split in half, a table running off the edge, an emoji replaced by an empty box.

Recent findings suggest that sitePoint covered the classic route back in 2015 with Creating PDFs from Markdown with Pandoc and LaTeX. That approach still works. But a lot has changed since then, and today there are several ways to get a clean PDF without installing a TeX distribution. This article compares them, then goes through the rendering problems you'll actually hit, with a fix for each.

Pandoc is still the Swiss Army knife. The simplest command is:.

In a recent development, by default, that goes through LaTeX, which means you need a TeX distribution installed (several gigabytes for a full one). The output is beautiful for prose and math, but LaTeX has strong opinions about layout, and customizing it means writing LaTeX.

Pandoc can also render through an HTML engine instead, which lets you style the PDF with CSS:.

Best for: long documents, academic writing, math, automated pipelines.

Watch out for: install size, Unicode handling with the default engine (more on that below).

It has been revealed that render the Markdown to HTML (any previewer, a static site, a GitHub page) and print it to PDF. It's free and already installed everywhere, but you inherit whatever the page looks like on screen: navigation bars, sidebars, and page breaks wherever they happen to fall.

Best for: quick, one-off exports of short documents.

Watch out for: zero control over page breaks unless the page ships print CSS.

Extensions like Markdown PDF for VS Code, or CLI tools like md-to-pdf, render your Markdown to HTML and print it with a headless Chromium:.

You get the same rendering quality as a browser, plus a config file for CSS, margins, headers and footers. The trade-off is a Node install and a downloaded Chromium.

Best for: developers who live in their editor or want CI-friendly exports.

Watch out for: the first run downloads a browser, and print CSS is still your job.

It has been revealed that the newest option is tools that do the whole conversion inside the browser tab: you paste or drop the .md file, preview the actual pages and download the PDF. The good ones don't upload your file anywhere, which matters for client documents and internal notes.

Best for: people who don't want to install anything, non-developers on your team, private documents.

Watch out for: many online converters do upload your file to a server; check before you paste anything confidential.

Whichever method you pick, the same handful of problems show up as soon as the document is longer than a page. Most of them are fixed with print CSS, which works in Pandoc's HTML engines, Chromium-based tools and any HTML you print from a browser.

A 20-line function cut after line 3, with the rest on the next page, is the most common complaint. The fix is to ask the renderer not to break inside the block:.

One caveat: a block longer than a full page has to break. For those, it's better to let it break cleanly than to push it to a upcoming page and leave a huge gap.

On screen, a long line in a code block scrolls horizontally. On paper, there's no scrollbar, so it's simply cut off. Wrap long lines in print:.

Tables with many columns overflow the page or get squeezed until every cell is one word per line. Three things help: a smaller font size for tables, a landscape page for the worst offenders, and avoiding breaks in the middle of short tables:.

If a table genuinely needs eight columns, consider whether it should be a table in the PDF at all, or an appendix in landscape.

A heading alone at the bottom of a page, with its content on the next one, looks broken. This rule keeps a heading attached to what follows it:.

Support for break-after: avoid varies between rendering engines, so test it with yours; when it isn't honored, a manual page break before the heading is the reliable fallback.

Markdown has no syntax for a page break. The usual trick is a raw HTML element that print CSS turns into a break:.

Some converters also recognize a comment like , which has the advantage of staying invisible when the same file is rendered on GitHub.

It has been revealed that images are inserted at their natural size, so a 4000-pixel screenshot spills off the page. Cap them:.

For blurry images, the problem is usually the opposite: a small screenshot stretched to page width. Export screenshots at 2x if they're going into a PDF.

Recent findings suggest that this one is specific to the LaTeX route. With the default pdflatex engine, Unicode characters outside its supported set produce errors or simply vanish. Switch to XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX and give it a font that actually contains the characters:.

Emoji are harder still in LaTeX and often need a dedicated package. HTML-based renderers handle both far better, because they use the operating system's font fallback just like a web page does.

Internal links ([see setup](#setup)) and external links should stay clickable. HTML-based renderers usually keep both. If yours doesn't, check that headings get IDs (most Markdown parsers add them) and that the PDF engine preserves link annotations.

Put together, these rules make a solid starting point for any HTML-based route:.

Save it as print.css and pass it to Pandoc (--css=print.css with an HTML engine), to md-to-pdf through its config, or include it in the HTML you print from the browser.

My rule of thumb after a lot of trial and error:.

A quick README or notes export, no install, private content: an in-browser converter. Full disclosure: this need is why I built the free Markdown to PDF converter on AwesomeToolkit, and it's what I use for this case now. It renders real A4 or Letter pages as you type, has an option to keep code blocks and tables whole, adds page numbers and a table of contents, and the conversion happens in the browser, so the file isn't uploaded anywhere.

Documentation in a repo, exported in CI: md-to-pdf or Pandoc with an HTML engine, plus the stylesheet above.

Long reports, math, academic formatting: Pandoc with XeLaTeX, using a font that covers every script in the document.

Something you'll print once and forget: the browser's Print to PDF is fine.

Industry observers note that whatever you choose, the biggest quality jump comes from the print rules, not the tool. Ten lines of CSS turn "it looks fine until page three" into a PDF you can actually send.

According to recent reports, yes. Your browser's Print to PDF works on any rendered Markdown, and in-browser converters do the whole conversion in a tab. Check that the converter processes files locally if the content is private.

In a recent development, the default pdflatex engine has limited Unicode support. Use --pdf-engine=xelatex or lualatex and set a font that contains the characters with -V mainfont= (and -V CJKmainfont= for CJK text).

In a recent development, markdown has no native syntax for it. Insert where you want the break, or use the page-break comment your converter supports.

Add pre { break-inside: avoid; } to your print CSS. Blocks longer than a page will still break, which is expected.

With HTML-based renderers, usually yes, both external links and links to headings inside the document. Test internal links in particular, since they depend on headings having IDs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before we dive deeper, let's do a quick recap on Enroute's architecture. Enroute separates compute from storage, like many modern databases. A cluster has three parts:.

When thinking about how many repositories we can fit on a single Enroute cluster, there are really two numbers to consider:.

While we had implemented some early optimizations already, two measurements highlighted where we still fell short:.

It has been revealed that every repository's log was its own state machine on a separate Raft log. Raft keeps a leader alive with heartbeats and when it fails, replaces it with an election, so every log had its own timers, votes, pre-votes and leader. With hundreds of thousands of repositories, that machinery became the workload.

In a recent development, it turns out that mature Multi-Raft-based systems have a well-known toolbox for this, which we began to make use of as best as possible. We allowed idle logs to go to sleep, moved liveness from each log to the node, and we woke a failed node's logs only as they were needed, to prevent kicking off thousands of leader elections at the same time when a single node fails.

These fixes worked. Together, they took the setup that had previously collapsed at 2,048 writers to about 14,000 pushes per second at 100,000 repositories with no failures.

However, taking a step back, it felt like we were just piling more complexity on top of the core Multi-Raft setup, which is already quite complex to start with. What's worse, this complexity was not only in code, but also directly translated into failure modes and edge cases.

In short, it became obvious that continuing on this path would lead to a system that would be much harder to understand and operate, which motivated us to start looking for alternatives.

In a recent development, looking at our setup at this point, most of the complexity came from the fact that we ran membership, and by extension leadership elections, on a per-repository basis. So we began looking at ways we could take leader election out of the per-repository log.

Sources indicate that there are a number of systems that put an external configuration master in charge of their replicas today. Among all of those, we liked Vertical Paxos (Lamport, Malkhi and Zhou, 2009) the best. The key insight behind it is that if something outside the log decides who's responsible for deciding its entries, the log itself needs no timers at all.

To apply this to Enroute, we introduced a singular "root log" that is responsible for tracking node membership per repository, while keeping the actual repository state inside each repository's log (which we'll call "shard log") and which is decided by a "sequencer" that's appointed via the root log.

On top of this, we then kept the parts from Raft that already worked well, and adopted specific pieces from Vertical Paxos.

What we keep from Raft is everything about how a log is written:.

What we adopt from Vertical Paxos is everything about how leadership changes:.

In our Multi-Raft setup, every ledger node was a member of every repository's Raft group, so each log lived on all of them. That also meant adding a ledger node added a copy of every log, without any way to spread the load across more nodes.

With this new design, thanks to the root log leader being in charge of appointing sequencers, it is straightforward to extend this responsibility to placement: The root log can now decide which ledger nodes to appoint as responsible for a certain shard log, which means we can distribute the responsibility for tracking repository metadata across a larger pool of ledger nodes.

Based on this idea, the root log leader we implemented is already capable of:.

Our proposal is to extend this placement logic further in upcoming releases to improve how Enroute balances load across ledger nodes and make this process more continuous rather than purely failover-driven.

Consensus protocols can be treacherous, and so a new consensus protocol naturally deserves suspicion. This is where the simpler design pays off: without an election in every log, the protocol is small enough to put under a model checker, which Raft with our fixes layered on top was not. We tested our new design in two ways.

Model checking the code the engine runs. The core protocol is written ("sans-IO" as the cool kids say) as a state machine without I/O: messages, proposals and clock ticks become inputs, and the pending messages and disk I/O tasks are output. This made it possible for us to use Stateright to exhaustively check the actual implementation rather than just a model, which simulates every possible interleaving of sequencers, appointments, reads, crashes and lost unsynced writes (within small bounds).

Jepsen against real processes. Here, our previous investment in setting up a Jepsen suite paid off. It drives Git clients while it partitions, kills and pauses nodes, with every ledger on LazyFS to simulate disk failures, while Elle checks ref reads for strict serializability. While working on our newly introduced consensus engine, it found two smaller non-safety-critical bugs not in the engine itself, but in how it integrated with the rest of the system (which is why the Stateright model checks didn't pick it up earlier). Luckily, both were easy to fix.

To find out how well these improvements worked, we tested our old implementation (0.3.0) against the new shard log based one (0.4.0), and grew each cluster in steps up to 100,000 repositories, and 0.4.0 on to 300,000.

The real win however doesn't even show in these numbers: Enroute's consensus layer now has far fewer moving parts, which makes it much easier to understand, operate and extend in the future as we continue our scaling journey.

With the newly won headroom on the ledger tier, here are the directions we're thinking of taking it next:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're thrilled to share that DeepInfra is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

According to recent reports, deepInfra joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

DeepInfra is a serverless AI inference platform offering one of the most cost-effective pricing per token in the industry. With a catalog of over 100 models, DeepInfra makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

DeepInfra supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-image, text-to-video, embeddings, and more. As part of this initial integration, DeepInfra is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as DeepSeek V4, Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and many more. Support for additional tasks (text-to-image, text-to-video, embeddings, and more) will roll out soon!

Read more about how to use DeepInfra as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the full list of models supported by DeepInfra here.

Follow DeepInfra on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/DeepInfra.

DeepInfra is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.11.2) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

Recent findings suggest that the following examples show how to use DeepSeek V4 Pro through DeepInfra. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to DeepInfra automatically.

It has been revealed that hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug DeepInfra-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a DeepInfra API key you're billed on your DeepInfra account.

According to recent reports, for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Latest Update: GhostScript CVE 2026-125396: "Upload2Shell"

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pwn

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies demonstrated how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter.
  • On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached.
  • That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026.

According to recent reports, our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies demonstrated how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software.

On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common.

That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent? We continued into Ghostscript's internals and found several independent bugs of varying impact. We reported them to Artifex and worked with affected platforms to harden their file processing. Some of those bugs are still being fixed.

This article follows one of the more interesting findings. Upload2Shell, now CVE-2026-125396, is a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. It gave us a write-what-where primitive: the ability to choose both the data written and its destination in native memory. A crafted document could use that control to alter the state enforcing -dSAFER and run commands as the rendering process.

Industry observers note that almost every application we tested with file uploads could be tricked into passing a file with a trusted extension to Ghostscript. A feature as routine as cropping an image or generating a preview could expose the interpreter. With the primitive working, we followed those conversion paths back out to their remote entry points.

It has been revealed that consider a PHP application generating a preview. Its code calls Imagick, the PHP binding to ImageMagick. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which may delegate the rendering to Ghostscript or another interpreter. The upload endpoint does not have to start gs itself; it only has to pass the file to a library that will.

Our WordPress-shaped preview proof reached that delegate through Imagick::readImage($input . '[0]'). The filename ended in .pdf, but the bytes were PostScript; ImageMagick handed them to Ghostscript under -dSAFER. The exploit also needed a Type 1 font file. In this delegate, it wrote the font to the scratch output path already authorized in currentpagedevice /OutputFile; another self-contained variant used Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device. Neither needed a pre-existing font file on the server.

Recent findings suggest that ghostscript can also be linked into an image-processing build as a library. In that arrangement, the interpreter runs inside the existing process instead of appearing as a separate gs command. Looking only for explicit Ghostscript calls in application code misses both kinds of indirect invocation.

Recent findings suggest that an application does not need to call gs itself. In our separate decoder tests, the following ordinary image calls reached Ghostscript when given EPS content, even when the file was named .png.

Industry observers note that image.open() alone only identified the file in our test. Loading pixels, cropping, or converting them started the renderer.

Our source audit also found image decoding calls in InvokeAI uploads, AUTOMATIC1111 img2img, and ComfyUI previews.

We tested the calls developers use after accepting an image. Across two controlled runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ghostscript installed, one matrix traced 145 benign calls across 29 image APIs and the other covered additional wrappers including Imagick and imageio. We also gave the PostScript sample a .png name. It was not a valid PNG; this tested whether the decoder trusted the name or inspected the bytes. The versions below describe the tested libraries, not every product that uses them.

The decoder matters. PHP GD, OpenCV, prebuilt Sharp, Jimp, Java ImageIO, and Go's standard image decoders did not start Ghostscript for these inputs. Copying or storing a file did not render it either; the later preview or conversion is the step to inspect.

Recent findings suggest that ghostscript renders both PDF and PostScript. PostScript is a Turing-complete programming language used to describe pages, so rendering a PostScript document means executing a program. Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox restricts that program's file access and command execution. Like seccomp, it limits what untrusted code can do, but the enforcement is different: -dSAFER relies on checks inside the interpreter rather than a kernel-enforced system-call filter.

That still leaves a large interpreter exposed to attacker-controlled programs. As with a JavaScript engine such as V8, running the language is expected; a memory-safety bug can let a program corrupt the engine running it. An attacker can develop and test that program as a PostScript file, then deliver it through an ordinary upload.

Those permission checks matter because the rendering process has access of its own. Its service account may be able to read application files, write to disk, and start other programs. The sandbox is supposed to keep an untrusted document from using that authority. Loading a font is one of the ordinary rendering operations that must respect this boundary.

It has been revealed that GPT 5.6 Sol, working with @PaulosYibelo, found the issue in .putgstringcopy, a helper in Resource/Init/gs_fonts.ps. Ghostscript implements parts of its own font loading in PostScript. This helper needed to write into protected font dictionaries, so it used an internal operation called .forceput.

Ordinary document code should not have that ability. The helper was bound and marked executeonly, protecting its implementation from direct inspection. But it still had to execute, and one of the operations before its privileged write could fail. The relevant sequence was:.

Sources indicate that the first line copies a string. The second performs the protected store and restores the allocation mode. The helper did not first check that its operands were of the expected types.

We registered a Type 1 font in Fontmap and loaded it with findfont. The font defined an ordinary Courier-derived face, but its loading code could see the font loader's operand stack. It replaced the filename string on that stack with a local array. In the global-to-local conversion branch, length and string allocation succeeded; copy then raised typecheck because its source was an array.

Sources indicate that the document's error handler returned with the stack prepared for the next operation in the already-bound helper. This is the operative excerpt from our proof:.

Sources indicate that the five pops discard the failing copy, its newly introduced destination string, our substituted filename, the loader's /PathLoad key, and the loaded font dictionary. They leave the saved allocation-mode boolean on the stack. Our chosen dictionary, key, and value follow it. Execution resumes at .forceput; the subsequent setglobal consumes the boolean. We never had to call the hidden operator directly.

One implementation detail made that recovered write more than a protected-dictionary edit. In psi/zgeneric.c, .forceput temporarily treats systemdict as local while it stores the value, then restores the dictionary's space flags. A local object can therefore pass the store check into a dictionary that survives a later restore.

Recent findings suggest that A protected dictionary write alone does not explain native code execution. The next step broke a separate rule: a reference must not remain usable after its object has been reclaimed.

PostScript distinguishes local and global virtual memory. Here, “virtual memory” refers to the interpreter's object spaces. A save records local memory state; a later restore discards objects created since that save. Global objects can survive that restoration.

Recent findings suggest that that creates a lifetime constraint. A surviving global dictionary must not keep a usable reference to a local object that restore will free. Otherwise, restoring the local space leaves the dictionary pointing into reclaimed storage.

Our recovered store let us create precisely that relationship:.

Sources indicate that the reference in the dictionary had not changed. What occupied the address had.

A small probe made the reuse visible before we touched native memory. This excerpt omits the font setup and error handler; findfont triggers the recovered .forceput, which places a local array in systemdict:.

In a recent development, the last read comes from Replacement; the write goes through the stale systemdict reference. If the freed allocation is reused, Replacement[1] reads 5151. The two references have reached the same bytes.

The native proof uses the same idea with a dangling 2,048-byte string and fresh arrays of integers. Each integer is 0x12345678. We scan the stale string for the marker's bytes, change its low byte from 0x78 to 0x79, then find the live array element that became 0x12345679. That identifies the overlapping slot; no absolute heap address has to be guessed.

On our 64-bit build, a Ghostscript ref occupies 16 bytes: eight bytes for its type, attributes, and size, followed by eight bytes for its value or pointer. We saved a valid integer ref for cleanup and the header of a valid writable string ref as a template. Then we placed currentdevice in the overlapping array slot, read its genuine device-reference pointer through the dangling string, and changed the live ref into a temporary string view over that pointer. The byte view let us follow Ghostscript's own pointers:.

Industry observers note that those structure offsets describe the tested x86-64 build; the address of each object came from a live interpreter reference. This is why the proof did not depend on a fixed process address. We restored the forged ref to its original integer form before exercising file or command access.

Recent findings suggest that we demonstrated native control in production image and document pipelines with a reversible change to an arithmetic operator. We copied the 16-byte mul reference, obtained a genuine sub reference, and replaced only the eight pointer bytes at offset 8 in the live mul ref. We invoked that same ref once and copied the original 16 bytes back. This was a C function-pointer change, not a PostScript definition of a new mul.

The returned page recorded the before, during, and after values:.

The middle result is 29 - 11. The captured proof output also recorded NATIVE_POINTER_OVERWRITE_MATCHED=true and NATIVE_DISPATCH_RESTORED=true. For most reports, we used a simpler proof that read /proc/version and returned its contents. The arithmetic test demonstrated native control; the file read demonstrated that we had crossed Ghostscript's file-access boundary.

According to recent reports, the same byte view gave us a target for command execution: Ghostscript's native path-control state. After walking the pointer chain above, Target was the forged string view over gs_lib_ctx_core_t. The decisive write in the proof was four PostScript put operations on native bytes:.

Those bytes were path_control_active. The proof read 1,0,0,0 before the write and 0,0,0,0 after it, then confirmed that .currentpathcontrolstate was false. -dSAFER was still on the Ghostscript command line; its native file-path check had been disabled in memory.

It has been revealed that that was not the only check. The proof first used the recovered .forceput to set the PostScript-side PermitFileWriting list to [ (*) ]. For %pipe%, parse_file_name() also consulted a cached LockFilePermissions flag. We loaded the font a third time, force-wrote that protected user parameter to false, and used save/restore to synchronize the cached value. The recorded sequence makes the separate gates visible:.

The bounded Debian print job ended with this command proof, writing only a marker in /var/tmp:.

Industry observers note that the scheduler recorded PIPE_RCE_STOPPED=false, and the marker file appeared on the print server. false here means the stopped block completed. The command ran as uid=7(lp), the renderer's account, not as the person who submitted the job.

With the interpreter primitive established, the next question was where a remote user could supply the document. We traced how popular applications invoked image and PDF processing. Three cases show how different the entry points could be.

An attacker only had to send a crafted email to someone using the Roundcube server and have the recipient view the message. The sender needed no Roundcube account. The recipient did not have to click or download the attachment: displaying the email triggered the server-side processing that ran our command.

Our attachment was declared as image/jpeg and named quarterly-results.jpg, but its contents were PostScript. Roundcube treated it as an image and automatically requested a thumbnail. The thumbnail path passed the attachment to ImageMagick, which invoked Ghostscript. The document ran our proof command as www-data and produced a thumbnail.

We reached the same Ghostscript interpreter while WordPress generated a preview for an uploaded PDF. In WordPress Core, media upload privileges were enough: Authors and higher roles have them by default. Plugins using WordPress's upload and preview functions exposed the same path. WordPress's CVE-2026-65640 advisory describes remote code execution on sites using Imagick and Ghostscript. On our Linux systems, that was the stack handling the uploads.

Recent findings suggest that plugins exposed that processing to visitors without an account. In Forminator, we used a public PDF field configured to store the upload in the Media Library. That caused WordPress to generate attachment metadata and enter the Imagick conversion path. Essential Addons for Elementor's public registration widget provided another route through its upload field. Both chains ran the command as the web-service user. Once the file reached the renderer, the font-loader flaw was the same.

According to recent reports, we also reached Ghostscript through CUPS on Debian 13 and other Linux distributions. On Debian 13, we sent an IPP Print-Job to a shared network queue that accepted jobs without authentication. CUPS passed our PostScript document to gstopdf, which started the distribution's Ghostscript with -dSAFER. The command ran on the print server as uid=7(lp).

It has been revealed that our RCE proof executed one fixed command and wrote a marker under /var/tmp. Requiring authentication on the queue blocked the unauthenticated submission. Shared queues that accept network print jobs without credentials expose the renderer to anyone who can reach them.

The Ghostscript CVE scores the interpreter flaw at 8.5 under CVSS 4.0. That rating uses a local attack vector. Our demonstrations reached the interpreter remotely, through both production services and the applications described here. CUPS supplied a network-exploitable print path; Roundcube supplied an email-based remote exploit; WordPress and its plugins supplied remotely exploitable upload paths. The recorded trials show that these chains were repeatable. The attacker could deliver the exploit remotely, despite the interpreter's local attack-vector classification.

Sources indicate that the first ten rows show Upload2Shell proofs in products or their shipped components. The rows after them trace more upload and preview paths. Each entry gives the access, tested stack or pinned source revision, and the processing step that matters.

It has been revealed that our Ghostscript research also reached Google, Dropbox, and other production services whose names are redacted. The table brings those production services together; the Dropbox and redacted findings have separate roots from the Type 1 bug described in this article.

It has been revealed that the renderer's account and the surrounding system controls determine what follows native memory control. That is why the table records process privileges and the observed result alongside the application name.

Industry observers note that here is a complete, self-contained PostScript proof of the native operator write described above. It writes its Type 1 font to Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device, triggers the font-loader flaw, reuses the freed allocation, changes a live mul reference to call sub, and restores the original bytes. No companion font file is needed.

Each step below points to its lines in the full file. The 29 × 11 check returns 319 before and after the write. While the pointer is changed, it returns 18, the result of subtraction. This proof demonstrates native memory control; the command-execution chain described above changes Ghostscript's path-control state instead.

Loading source… Open the complete file.

Sources indicate that the file changes native memory inside the rendering process. It does not execute a shell command or touch host files. On the fixed 10.08.0 build, the dangling-reference lookup failed before the pointer write.

It has been revealed that artifex's first fix checks the operands before .putgstringcopy can fail in copy. That closes the error path we used to recover the privileged store. A subsequent change moves the helper into C and removes its dependence on .forceput.

The first patch also explains why this kind of operation has been difficult to remove. Artifex was already working to eliminate or minimize its use. As the maintainer put it:.

“it isn't easy to undo 30 years worth of assumptions in the code.” Ken Sharp, Artifex, in the fix for bug 709684.

Industry observers note that an internal font loader needed a write that ordinary document code could not perform. An error exposed that authority to the document, and the document used it to violate an object-lifetime rule. The final memory corruption depended on assumptions made at several different layers.

Recent findings suggest that the applications had their own opportunities to interrupt the chain. WordPress released its Core mitigation in 7.0.4 on 12 August, with backports to older supported branches. Its application CVE and the Ghostscript CVE address different points in the processing path. For the CUPS route, queue authentication controls who can submit the document. A policy that prevents a renderer from starting a shell can limit what happens even after the interpreter is compromised.

The fix has to reach the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not upgrade a separate copy of Ghostscript inside an existing container image or application bundle. A document worker can therefore keep using vulnerable code after the host's package has been replaced.

Sources indicate that application hardening can close a route into the interpreter as well. The Roundcube sequence illustrates why the order of operations matters: checking a file's real type after generating its thumbnail gives the renderer the first chance to interpret it. For each downstream service, the useful question is what changed in the path from the submitted file to the rendering process.

Sources indicate that artifex released the root fix in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on 8 September 2026. Many distributions have since shipped it, either in that release or as a backport to an older version. Ubuntu published fixes for seven releases; Debian patched Trixie and its development branches.

Industry observers note that the coverage is uneven. As of 12 November, Debian still listed Bookworm as vulnerable, Amazon Linux listed a pending fix, and several SUSE branches remained affected or in progress. Applications on those branches can still expose the flaw when their file-processing path reaches the affected Ghostscript package. A distribution name or a recent patch to another Ghostscript CVE is not enough to establish that this bug is fixed.

The tables below record the package status for this specific flaw. Older version numbers can include a backported fix; a published fixed version does not establish that every application or container has adopted it.

It has been revealed that as of 12 November 2026, the following vendor trackers still listed a vulnerable, affected, or pending Ghostscript package for this exact flaw. These labels describe package status, not a tested remote application path. Check the package actually installed or bundled by each service.

We did not establish whether current RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages contain the .putgstringcopy fix.

Ubuntu's USN-8949-1, published on 21 October 2026, describes our font-operand finding and lists fixed Ghostscript packages for seven releases. The notice predates the CVE assignment, so it labels this finding “No CVE number.” These are package fixes, not additional remote application tests.

Recent findings suggest that debian's tracker records the first fixed source version for Trixie and unstable. The testing branch later received the upstream-fixed package. Debian 12 remains listed vulnerable in the vendor-status table above.

In a recent development, the records below show packages containing upstream Ghostscript 10.08.0 or an advisory-listed fixed build. A package appearing here does not establish the first fixed date for every architecture or branch.

Fixed Ghostscript builds also reached Windows and macOS packaging channels. The availability of a package does not tell us which Ghostscript binary a particular application uses.

The dependency problem is easy to miss from the top of an application. Several layers below, a file may enter PostScript or another interpreter that never appeared in the application's security review. A review that checks only whether the upload handler accepts trusted file types can miss a vulnerability in the code that eventually processes them. A penetration test that stops at the same boundary has the same blind spot.

Alongside this Type 1 problem, our broader Ghostscript audit reached production services at Dropbox and other redacted vendors through separate findings. Each program paid its maximum bounty. Their case studies will explain the individual root causes and proofs once we have permission to publish the technical details. The series is organized around the underlying bugs as well as the products.

Industry observers note that wordPress released its mitigation on 12 August. Artifex authored the Ghostscript fix on 2 September, committed it on 7 September, and released 10.08.0 on 8 September. We completed the Debian network CUPS proof on 17 September. The Ghostscript CVE was published on 9 November in US Eastern time.

The Debian 13 CUPS chain will be the first full case study and PoC in this series. The other product writeups will follow, with the build, delivery path, exploit result, and vendor response for each. We will add their links to the tables as they appear.

It has been revealed that we expect other researchers to find more applications affected by this flaw. The useful place to look is the processing that follows an accepted file: thumbnail generation, metadata extraction, document import, and print conversion. Each can hand an attacker-controlled document to a process with access the sender does not have. Upload2Shell let the document use that access for itself.
