📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified on November 21, 2026 that Levent Alpöge’s 17-million-line Lean library correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, following a day of compilation, statement-matching, and proof-kernel checks. Their joint statement was endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

The certification follows Alpöge’s announcement on November 20, 2026, in which he said he discovered and formalized the proof while working with Claude. The release contained only the Lean formalization; Alpöge viewed a conventional write-up at this stage as a huge, unreadable document and planned to understand, simplify, and explain the mathematics properly.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib, the community’s library of formalized mathematics. The statement being proved was already part of Mathlib and had been vetted by experts in Lean and number theory, addressing the requirement that the formal statement express the intended hypothesis. Dozens of people reported compiling the library without errors or build failures and reproducing the same raw proof export.

Industry observers note that to check the theorem’s identity, a community-added challenge file isolated the Riemann Hypothesis statement and imported only Mathlib. Comparator and con-leche’s comparison mode independently confirmed that Alpöge’s theorem matched that statement exactly. The raw proof export was checked with Lean’s official kernel, con-leche, con-ron, and additional third-party checkers written in different programming languages.

Those checks ran on an inert export, beyond the reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean sources. Con-leche and con-ron also have formal proofs, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, addressing concerns that a flaw in Lean’s logic could be exploited.

Andrew Sutherland’s MIT verification record, last updated at 12:55 UTC on November 21, 2026, reports that all 175,187 modules compiled with zero errors using Lean and Mathlib version 4.33.1; his checks were run with Claude Code. An axiom audit found that the five headline theorems depended only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, with no axioms declared outside Lean core. Nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, and con-leche each accepted the full exported proof, lean4lean accepted every compiled module, and con-leche’s comparison mode matched every challenge statement.

At that page’s cutoff, the Lean default and paranoid kernel checks on the export and the full lake comparator run remained in progress. Older bundled con-leche and con-ron binaries exited without a verdict because they did not support one reflexive inductive type, not because they rejected the proof. Sutherland also disclosed that the build ran on unsandboxed cloud machines and that its export hash had not been compared with one from a sandboxed lake build; a passing result still relies on the kernels used and on Mathlib’s definitions representing their intended mathematics.

It has been revealed that the central theorem uses Mathlib’s formal definition: every zero of the Riemann zeta function other than the trivial zeros at negative even integers must have real part one-half. The separate condition s ≠ 1 appears because Mathlib assigns the zeta function a conventional value at its pole. The submission also verifies Generalized Riemann Hypothesis statements for Dirichlet L-functions across all moduli and characters; Sutherland expressly excludes Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions, and general automorphic L-functions from the checked scope.

Alpöge’s account assigns Claude a role in discovery as well as formalization: he guided the work from a toy setting into an analogous target situation before Claude outpaced him near the finish. In one example, Claude suggested that a von Mangoldt sum of length X should use a chain of theta lifts of length X, a technical choice Alpöge highlights in his explanation of the argument.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge describes the current argument as extremely long, expects substantial simplification, and is still working to understand and explain it. His account describes human guidance and Claude’s technical contributions, with both formalizing the arguments without extra assumptions. The certification concerns the formal artifact; that account supplies the basis for describing Claude’s role, rather than demonstrating an autonomous solution.

The certification resolves the formal-checking question without resolving the explanatory one. Whether the proof’s fresh ideas can be simplified and absorbed by mathematicians remains the central open question around the verified Lean library.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service. An AI coding agent had exposed the private-repository credential used in the download while the organization was developing its public xorl GitHub repository.

Customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository. They involved requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026 and July 14, 2026.

The coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development. Together AI’s automated scanning detected the exposure, and the tech giant reverted the commit. During that exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored samples.

The sequence makes clear that detecting and reverting the commit did not prevent the credential from being used during the exposure window. The model names establish which requests were sampled, while the repository credential explains how the stored prompts became accessible.

It has been revealed that after the download, the party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested whether they were valid. Five of the tested credentials were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. The searches and validity tests show that the activity extended to possible reuse of secrets contained in prompts, creating a risk beyond disclosure of the prompt text itself.

According to recent reports, together AI worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement. The company said its review has not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident, that it has no reason to believe the data was leaked further, and that it understands the data has now been deleted.

According to recent reports, customer impact still depends on the content of the samples. The review is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed, and Together AI will contact affected customers directly as needed with findings relevant to them.

Together AI’s response includes scoped or short-lived credentials and keyless access where supported, credential checks on all pull requests, and updated development processes governing the use of AI coding agents. The firm said the credential measures are designed to reduce the potential impact of exposure, while the other changes add controls around pull requests and coding-agent development.

Zero data retention, abbreviated ZDR, is now the default setting for latest accounts. Together AI recommends that customers handling sensitive prompt data enable ZDR in their account settings and provides security@together.ai for questions about the incident or its potential impact on an organization.

In a recent development, the incident connects credential safety in AI-assisted development with the retention of customer prompts for testing. Together AI has documented controls for both, but the ongoing content review remains the decisive step in establishing what the exposure means for customers and which notifications are necessary.

Profiling in PyTorch (Part 1): A Beginner's Guide to torch.profiler

📅 29 May 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.
  • The catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp.
  • This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What you cannot profile, you cannot optimize.

Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.

The catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp. The traces are dense walls of colored rectangles. The events carry intimidating names. Most tutorials assume you can already read them. So even when we know we should be profiling, opening a trace can feel like a chore best left for later (or for someone else). This post, and the series it kicks off, is our attempt to lower that on-ramp.

This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

It has been revealed that we document the journey from a beginner's point of view. No prerequisites apart from basic PyTorch. Treat this as a leisurely read with some "Aha!" moments. The structure of the post is intentionally question-led: we open a trace, ask "wait, why is that happening?", and chase the answer until something clicks. By the end you should know:.

Before we begin, two definitions that will make everything below read better:.

You don't usually have to write GPU kernels yourself; when you use a PyTorch operation, it is automatically translated to one or more kernels that do the job on GPU.

With those two ideas in your back pocket, let's start asking questions.

Here is the entire script that we use for the post: 01_matmul_add.py. We recommend opening this script in a separate tab and walk through the code step by step. We use the NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to setup a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using the Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.(Note: The traces in this blog were generated using PyTorch 2.13. If you are using a different version, some trace details like CompiledFxGraph might differ or be absent.).

As correctly quipped by Dr. Sara Hooker, just as we are primarily made up of water, Deep Neural Networks are primarily made up of matrix multiplies. As fundamental as they are, it would be a shame to start our profiling journey with anything else.

The matrix addition along with the matrix multiplication mimics how weights and biases interact in a neuron. This addition (pun intended) will help us understand how it paves the way for compilation later in the post.

To profile, we will be using the torch.profiler module. The steps involved are:.

The profiler exports two distinct artifacts:.

Recent findings suggest that let's see the two in action with our first execution. (Here is the entire 01_matmul_add.py script).

It is recommended to run this script on a machine with a GPU.

If you run the above script (on a GPU machine) you will find a folder traces/01_matmul_add with the two artifacts:.

In a recent development, the .txt file holds the profiler table. Upon opening the file, as shown in Figure 1, one would be greeted with a big table with the first column consisting of the events that were triggered inside the scope of profile.

It has been revealed that the other columns are related to the time the event takes on the CPU or GPU or any other device(s) specified in activities within torch.profiler.profile. Look at which events take the most amount of time, and try to intuitively understand if that event should in fact take that time. It is also crucial to look at the column "# of Calls" which dictates how many times the event was triggered.

While we are at it, let's also talk about "Self CPU/CUDA" vs "CPU/CUDA total". The "Self" columns measure time spent only inside the event itself, excluding its children. The "total" columns include the event and all of its children together. So if you look at the "CPU total" of matmul_add, it consists of the time it took on self plus the children events it triggered. This is an important nuance to note.

If you look at the last two lines out of the table you would notice that the profiler tells us that.

Industry observers note that the CPU time is in ms while the GPU time is in us. To put things in perspective, the time spent on GPUs (the kernel ampere_bf16_s16816gemm...) is less than 1% of the time spent on the CPU (the matmul_add operation). The GPU stays idle most of the time, which is an immediate red flag. The reason this happens is that the GPU can compute a small matmul very rapidly, so our code spends most of the time preparing the kernels, launching them on the GPU, sending the data to multiply and gathering the results. This concept is known as an overhead-bound algorithm.

The easiest way to move out of this regime is to use bigger matrix multiplications.

The last two lines in Figure 2 are:.

It has been revealed that both times are in ms, which means we have materialized more GPU time just by increasing the size of the matrix multiplications. If you look at Figure 2 you would also notice that the most CUDA time is now taken by the GPU kernel (ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_..) and not by the CPU operation that introduced it (matmul_add). This means that we were indeed able to move from overhead bound to compute bound.

Industry observers note that we now move into visualising the dispatch chain, which lives inside the .json artifacts. You can upload them to Perfetto UI and see the traces, or you can use uvx trace-util -f traces -b /traces to generate the Perfetto links directly.

According to recent reports, in Figure 3, we see the profiler trace for the matrix multiplication and addition. Here the bar width indicates the duration of an event, the vertical nesting is the call hierarchy, the CPU lane denotes the events that happen on the CPU, while the GPU lane highlights the actual kernel executions. One might also notice the empty spaces which are the waiting or idle time.

The script was run with default configurations which are:.

With Perfetto we suggest using the keyboard for quicker access to the trace. One could use "W A S D" for navigating the trace.

It has been revealed that there are two lanes in Figure 4, one for the CPU activity and one for the GPU activity. In the CPU lane one would notice three profile steps (starting from ProfilerStep#2). This comes from the schedule.

The wait skips noisy initializations (ProfilerStep#0), warmup runs through the profiler without recording (ProfilerStep#1), and active is what highlights up in trace. One can find the schedule being used in the script here.

Let's put on our detective hats and investigate the trace and ask some questions.

In a recent development, in Figure 5, we notice that ProfileStep#2 takes more time compared to the other steps, and upon looking closely you would see a similar pattern with the matmul_add annotation as well. The smoking gun is inside the annotation, not the annotation itself:.

In a recent development, that ~228 µs shown in Figure 6 is the "dead window" between entering record_function("matmul_add") and PyTorch actually dispatching aten::matmul. This can happen for multiple reasons, including workspace allocations, cuBLAS (NVIDIA’s proprietary, GPU-accelerated library for performing fundamental linear algebra operations) heuristics, or lazy module loading. We can either look away or run some more warmup steps before we profile (which is the standard).

In terms of profiling, warmup is when you run the events a couple of times before actually profiling it. The pre-work done by the GPU (including the above pointers) are one time efforts which we do not want to profile. In our example, we have two warmup stages, one where we actually loop over the function before entering the profiler, and two inside the profiler which is achieved by the warmup argument. In this section, we have enabled the actual iterations along with the schedule.

Perfetto Trace for 64x64 with Warmup.

In a recent development, in Figure 7 we see that each profile step takes a similar time, but this does not mean we were able to optimize the one time overheads. We warmed up the runs so that the overheads were not profiled. We think that closing this section abruptly without a hint to solving this would do injustice to the reader, so here is a link to read about further optimizing launch overheads.

In Figure 8, we see that the CPU and GPU lanes have an offset of around 2.5 ms: this is the delay after the CPU submits the CUDA kernels and the time they actually start executing. One might think the warmup stage combined with the schedule's wait and warmup should keep a GPU busy and would diminish the offset.

To uncover what is really happening, let's change our schedule a little:.

Figure 9 shows us that there is an Activity Buffer Request in the GPU lane before any operation. Let's zoom in a little more.

In a recent development, upon zooming into the GPU trace, we notice that the matmul and add kernels for ProfileStep#0 (the CPU trace of which is not visible in the Figure) happen one after the other, while the kernels for ProfileStep#1 have a window in between. The best explanation for this is that there was an overflow of buffers, and another buffer request (a request to allocate some memory on the GPU VRAM) was issued during the kernel execution.

The best way to rule out other possibilities is to profile for more iterations and see whether a similar window appears in other parts of the trace. To do that we run with active=20.

As shown in Figure 11, we see a similar trend in ProfileStep#1. This is aligned with our previous findings, and we can safely conclude that it was indeed another buffer request.

Industry observers note that in Figure 12, we see the nested CPU calls. This is an important visualization, where one gets to understand what a chain of dispatch really looks like.

We begin with ProfileStep# which encapsulates the profiling step. Due to us annotating the step, we see the matmul_add row. The matmul_add consists of two aten calls, one for matrix multiplication and one for matrix addition.

Industry observers note that the aten::matmul is the ATen-level dispatch that those user-facing PyTorch matmul calls land on. aten::mm is the 2D matrix-matrix multiply backend.

Sources indicate that it is very interesting to note how PyTorch calls aten::bmm (batched matrix multiplication) if we add the batch axis to our matrices. Let's take a detour and see the aten::bmm in action.

Recent findings suggest that in Figure 13, upon adding the batch axis to the inputs, aten::matmul now encapsulates a bunch of other prerequisite CUDA runtime calls along with aten::bmm (instead of aten::mm). This also hints at the heuristics that cuBLAS needs to do in order to dispatch the right (most suitable) kernel for the program.

In the rest of the post, we will be working with simple 2D matrices, unless otherwise mentioned.

We notice that for aten::mm there are two CUDA Runtime calls, namely cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor (boxed in Figure 14) and cudaLaunchKernel, while for aten::add there is only the cudaLaunchKernel.

cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor is a planning call and is purely CPU side. It asks: "given a kernel function, a chosen block size, and a chosen dynamic shared memory size, how many blocks of this kernel can simultaneously reside on one SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)?".

This begs the question, why do we need planning for matmul and not for add?

To understand this, we have to look at the kernel's resource footprint. If you click on the GPU kernels, you will be able to inspect the resource footprint for the respective kernel.

Sources indicate that in Figure 15, we note that for matrix multiplication the registers per thread and shared memory are dynamic (based on the size of the matrix). cuBLAS ships hundreds of kernel variants, and each has a heuristic-driven launch path that needs runtime information about hardware capacity. The occupancy query is part of that heuristic. Conceptually, we can think of GPU-accelerated matmuls as working on independent tiles: how many tiles we use and how big each tile needs to be depends on the matrices and the hardware. Modern algorithms are way more complicated than that, but this is still a good reference framework.

From Figure 16 we see that the footprint of addition notes 32 registers and zero shared memory. That fits trivially. There's nothing to query, because no hardware resource is going to limit occupancy. The kernel is, by design, resource-light.

Industry observers note that you can use this as a quick diagnostic when reading any trace. Scan the CPU lane for cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor. Each occurrence flags a "heavyweight, adaptively debuted" kernel, usually a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiplication), conv, or similar. The kernels without a preceding occupancy query are the elementwise/reduction crowd that PyTorch launches mechanically.

cudaDeviceSynchronize blocks the CPU until all GPU work on this device finishes. The profiler emits this sync at the end of the active window to flush events. Without it, kernel timings would be missing.

A 1.78 ms sync covering 26 µs of real GPU work tells you this run was 98% idle. That's the textbook overhead-bound symptom.

We already know from the profiler table analysis (above) that providing bigger matrices to our algorithm moves it out from the overhead-bound region to being compute-bound.

Let's run the command and dive deeper into the traces.

It has been revealed that in Figure 17, we notice that the matmul kernel for ProfileStep#3 takes longer on the GPU than the other steps. This is particularly interesting to note, because the other kernels debuted were the exact same, which means there were no cuBLAS heuristics involved. There are no scheduling gaps, the CPU launches are normal, and it is not a profiler artifact.

This trace in Figure 17 makes a useful point that's easy to miss in idealized examples: kernel runtimes are not constants, even on the same hardware environment running identical code on identical data.

In a recent development, let's make this more concrete by modifying the script a little. We run the iteration 20 times, capturing each of the steps.

Figure 18 reveals a similar finding. While each kernel was the exact same, they time differently. The different compute times can be blamed on a bunch of reasons:.

Industry observers note that A reader who only saw the average would conclude that a matmul took ~1 ms (mean of 5 = 1084 µs); a reader who looked at the trace would see that the matmul takes ~580 µs except when the GPU throws a fit. Those are very different mental models, and only one of them is correct.

Working with torch.compile has always amazed us. One writes normal eager PyTorch code, but PyTorch tries to capture tensor-heavy regions, turn them into graphs, optimize them, and run generated code. The default backend is usually TorchInductor, and the broad pipeline is:.

In this section, we talk about compilation and look at the profiler traces.

The args.compile flag triggers the following code:.

In Figure 19, we see the upcoming CPU rows named Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 which points us to the compiled functions being used.

Looking at Figure 20 we ask the question, did we actually fuse the multiplication and addition operations together into one?

This is operator fusion at the graph level. Inductor took our torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) and rewrote it into a single aten::addmm(b, x, w) call. The important thing to note here is that it did not produce a latest fused CUDA kernel. The actual GPU work is still ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_bf16_128x256_ldg8_f2f_stages_64x3_nn, the same cuBLAS kernel eager mode used. So the "fusion" here is at the dispatcher level, not at the kernel level.

In a recent development, pyTorch provides the torch.addmm function that does what we did in two steps, that is multiply and add. We encourage the reader to look at the traces of this function and comment your observations in the comments below!

While we know in theory what happens when we compile our functions it is equally crucial to see it in action. Let's look at the CPU-side hierarchy which reflects torch.compile's runtime architecture.

Recent findings suggest that torchDynamo Cache Lookup is where Dynamo checks that the current call still matches what was compiled with the same input shapes, dtypes, devices, and tensor metadata. If anything mismatched, Dynamo would recompile. This cost is paid every call, even after compilation.

Torch-Compiled Region is the wrapper that "enters" the compiled version. AOTDispatcher Runtime Wrapper Prologue is AOT Autograd's runtime wrapper. Even though we don't need gradients here, AOTDispatcher is always in the stack handling tensor metadata, view tracking, and would set up the backward pass if requires_grad were true.

It has been revealed that ## Call CompiledFxGraph is where the actual generated code runs. The string after "CompiledFxGraph" is the content hash of the FX graph. It's the same across all three active steps, confirming cache hits.

You can find the generated code on disk under /tmp/torchinductor_/fxgraph keyed by this hash, useful when you want to read the Triton/C++ that Inductor actually produced.

Looking at the traces in Figure 21, we were really happy to notice only one cudaLaunchKernel per step. This observation was directly contradicting what we were seeing in the GPU trace. There were still two kernels being launched per step, namely the Memcpy DtoD (Device -> Device) and the GEMM. Going back to the CPU trace, we noticed that we had completely missed the cudaMemcpyAsync dispatch.

In a recent development, addmm computes out = α·A·B + β·C, and cuBLAS's GEMM-with-bias-add epilogue writes into a destination buffer that needs to already contain the bias. An epilogues can be thought of all the operations that happen after a GEMM. In the world of deep-learning we constantly come up with GEMM-Epilogues like activations, bias addition, normalization and many more. This is why there are cuBLAS GEMM-with- kernel variants.

If you use different modes for torch.compile you would notice different kernel variants being released. You can try it for yourself and add a comment below about your observations!

So Inductor-generated code does:.

According to recent reports, the result is mathematically still the same. The bias add isn't free, as we pay a memcpy upfront plus a slightly more expensive GEMM epilogue.

Sources indicate that the fusion one might have hoped for, where x·w + b (here out = α·A·B + β·C) collapses into a single kernel with no extra memory traffic, isn't what happened. Inductor preserved the two memory-touching operations, it just relabeled the bias copy as a memcpy and the addition as a GEMM epilogue.

A truly fused implementation would skip the memcpy. That's what FlashAttention-style hand-written kernels do, and what Inductor can do via Triton codegen, but for a 4096×4096 bf16 matmul, Inductor evidently decided "use cuBLAS, do the bias via epilogue setup" was the best path.

This is the easiest thing to miss when comparing an eager and a compiled run:.

torch.compile is roughly 2× more expensive on the CPU per step. That's because every call walks the full Dynamo > AOTAutograd > Inductor stack, on top of the same aten::addmm dispatch we have anyway. The compile pipeline is built for ML models with dozens of ops where the per-call overhead amortizes (for a single op it's a tax).

torch.compile has a mode argument. It is for the reader to take home as an assignment to read the documentation and come up with a mode that could take the CPU overhead down. 🤗.

A quick reference for the patterns we walked through. The idea is: if you see this in a trace, this is what it usually means.

In a recent development, we started with a tiny matmul + add and used it as an excuse to learn how to read a PyTorch profiler. Along the way we picked up a few mental models that travel well to bigger workloads. This was the first stop in the Profiling PyTorch series. In the posts that follow, we will gradually leave this two-op toy behind and walk up the ladder of complexity, looking at larger building blocks and, eventually, real models.

Thanks to Noe Flandre, Suvaditya Mukherjee, and Vidit Ostwal for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

According to recent reports, the blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗.

Thanks a bunch for this blog post series -really much needed! Especially the Trace reading cheatsheet sections are very beneficial.

There are some parts I have been thinking about:.

Firstly, thanks for the questions. To answer 2 you are right, the context manager should take care of it, but I personally like putting an extra sync to be sure. You can omit it in your own scripts.

Coming to 1, this was really interesting, I had to go back to docs to get more idea. You are right with your observation about cudaMemcpyAsync vanishing and only one kernel launch ..._ldg8_relu_f2f_stages_64x3_nn. It turns out that the fresh kernels is a relu family kernel, which does the EPILOGUE properly where it falls under the contract of using a bias and broadcasting it across rows. Previously the bias was 2D and did not fall under the correct EPILOGUE contract, and hence there was an extra cudaMemcpyAsync.

Thanks for the kind words! Glad you liked it.

Sources indicate that good read! Helped introduce me to the world of GPUs and lower level stuff. While I understood the shape of things, it made me realise I have a lot of gaps in my knowledge wrt to this aspect of ML.

Recent findings suggest that it would be great if the PyTorch version that was used was mentioned here as well. I was stuck because my trace was not displaying CompiledFxGraph. It worked on Colab but not on my local machine. I was using PyTorch 2.8.0, which does not show CompiledFxGraph in the trace.

Industry observers note that ah! This is an vital pointer I missed in the blog. I was using 2.13 throughout the post. Thanks for catching it. Do you mind sending a PR to the blog (github.com/huggingface/blog) and I could merge it! 🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that openRouter declared on November 22, 2026, that it had off-boarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting under which prompts and responses are not stored. It also notified all potentially affected customers.

The findings did not show a breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself, the firm noted. The removals covered providers flagged by researchers and other endpoints withdrawn as a precaution. Its public list links notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI, but does not identify them as the three off-boarded providers; not all affected providers have published notices.

In research published on November 19, 2026, Dragos described submitting approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary credentials to widely used AI services from July through November 2026, then monitoring subsequent activity. The tests produced evidence that data from at least three AI providers was exposed, that marketplace resellers viewed and retained customer prompts through standard logging, and that some providers appeared to disregard privacy settings or published policies.

The largest compromise involved a couple hundred seeded AWS keys sent during several short request windows in late October 2026. Some keys came from requests rejected before a model ran, which Dragos interpreted as evidence that copying occurred when requests first reached the provider rather than during model processing. The bait keys were subsequently used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

The routing findings matter because every organization along a multi-hop path can see the complete prompt and response. Dragos traced about 2,000 inference routes: several hundred included an unidentified system, while in a handful, a company absent from the advertised path fetched the test image. Dragos also reported that one unnamed Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026, including roughly two-thirds marked no-data-collection or ZDR.

Novita’s privacy notice mentioned a routing configuration problem broadened an API forwarding path intended for specific customers, sending some MiniMax requests to MiniMax’s official API rather than Novita-hosted infrastructure. Requests made directly through Novita or routed through OpenRouter between May 28, 2026, and November 11, 2026, may have had their contents accessed or retained by a third party. Novita suspended the affected models. The researcher observed accesses to test URLs and hostnames but no use of AWS test-key markers; automated content review may have been involved, an assessment Novita is checking with MiniMax.

In a recent development, phala’s preliminary incident report, published on November 10, 2026, advised users whose DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests were routed to Phala by OpenRouter from 00:00 UTC on October 21, 2026, to 05:35 UTC on November 8, 2026, to treat the contents as exposed and rotate included secrets. The attacker chained a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that trusted loopback access without independently authenticating callers. A similar access pattern gave the attacker control of an inference VM, making in-flight request data visible during processing.

Phala confirmed canary misuse only for requests sent on October 21–22, 2026, but kept the wider window because the tests sampled requests and could not reveal every possible data-access event. Containment was completed on November 8, 2026, and a full-platform audit found no evidence of compromise affecting other models or products. The investigation and verification of remediation remain active, with a full root-cause analysis planned.

It has been revealed that together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after an AI coding agent committed a credential for a private Hugging Face repository to the public xorl GitHub repository. Collected for routine software testing with authorization, the samples came from MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 requests, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026, and July 14, 2026. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, including five Dragos canary credentials.

Recent findings suggest that together remarked it has not identified additional prompt leakage beyond the incident, but its review of affected prompt contents and determination of which customers require direct notification remain ongoing. Its changes include scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on all pull requests, ZDR by default for new accounts and updated development rules for AI coding agents.

OpenRouter is adapting the researchers’ testing approach for ongoing checks and technically verifying network paths to identify requests and responses that may be forwarded to third parties. Removed endpoints will require appropriate assurances and validation before regaining ZDR eligibility.

Novita is verifying the affected processing paths, pursuing deletion of any retained data with MiniMax and improving Partner API labeling and disclosures of relevant providers’ retention policies. For routed inference, the consequence is that ZDR eligibility now rests on validation of the actual request path alongside provider assurances. OpenRouter’s continuing checks leave one central operational question: whether ongoing testing can expose undisclosed forwarding and retention failures before they affect customer data.

#57666. Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic

Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic

📅 01 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Guides have aided humanity throughout history.
  • According to recent reports, numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption.
  • Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Guides have aided humanity throughout history. Prehistoric civilizations understood that the sun and the moon could be used to navigate vast distances on land and the high seas. Over time, various journeys facilitated the production of maps for better planning and faster travel time to repeat destinations. Centuries later, the introduction of the compass enabled seagoers to achieve greater accuracy in seeking unexplored destinations. And today, GPS navigation apps guide our every journey. In today’s world of agentic AI, AI agents, admittedly, have the potential to enable scalable AI adoption, transforming industries as we know them. However, an intelligent guide, agentic logic, is needed to realize this potential by fueling high agent quality, cost-effectiveness, and consequent end-user trust.

Enterprise Workflows & Use Cases.

According to recent reports, numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption. [1] [2] To better understand this phenomenon and the associated assertion, some analysis of enterprise workflows is required. These workflows are:.

A. Dynamic and long-runningB. Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC. Oftentimes are constrained by business policies and/or regulations.

For an agent to function effectively, given these above characteristics, naturally demands an expanded model context, which state-of-the-art frontier LLMs certainly possess, but at what tradeoff? Increased hallucinations, token consumption? Further, can LLMs be equipped with an intelligent guide, GPS, to enable agentic AI execution at the core of the workflow, driving more desirable outcomes? We tested these hypotheses by designing and building agents, equipped with pertinent agent logic, for IBM offerings fully considering the above characteristics. These offerings pertain to some of the most challenging tasks confronting subject matter experts who own various stages of the enterprise software delivery lifecycle for mission critical workloads including:.

Before examining each of these domains in detail, let us define what characterizes agent logic. Agent logic is software primitives, such as knowledge graphs, algorithms, program analysis libraries, which operate at the agentic layer (within an agent harness) and can intentionally steer the LLM in the direction of the enterprise workflow, reducing the context space. In so doing, have strong tendency to drive more performant outcomes in a more cost-effective manner. Let us now examine how agent logic is able to achieve such outcomes in each of the above four domains.

Recent findings suggest that IBM watsonx Code assistant for Z (WCA4Z), used to accelerate mainframe application development and modernization with AI and automation, is equipped with an App Insights agent for application understanding - one of the primary focus areas of enterprise clients running mission critical workloads on IBM mainframe. This agent leverages deep static analysis across the application and stores a pre-indexed representation in a database schema that spans hundreds of interrelated tables with complex semantics, allowing the agent to retrieve precise, structured already available information; thereby improving answer accuracy, reducing token usage, and minimizing back-and-forth interactions with the language model (Mistral Medium 250B in this instance). This approach when applied to multiple mission-critical legacy systems (up to 1M lines of code and 1K programs) maintains marginally superior app understanding performance with ~30× lower token consumption than a baseline frontier LLM-only approach.

It has been revealed that aster is an IBM proprietary program analysis and data pre- and post-processing-based library utilized for agent-based generation of unit, integration, API and change-based tests; which from analysis of multiple developer communities achieves higher developer ratings compared with various open-sourced tools or developer-written tests. Based on the latter and superior line, branch and method coverage benchmarks compared with similar open-sourced tools (integration tests) and zero-shot LLMs and coding agents (unit tests), all tested on open-sourced applications, we have been running Aster in pre-production mode on 75+ java IBM CIO applications (up to 560+ classes and 67K+ lines of code) with Devstral 24B model. Steady-state results to date yield +20% - 45% improvement in line, branch and method coverage coupled with superior performance on a subset of these apps compared with state-of-the-art coding agent with orders of magnitude lower token consumption (up to 15×). The rationale for these results is that the program analysis output (used to prompt and “focus” the LLM) coupled with sub-agents for augmenting coverage and remediating runtime and compilation errors enable a more performant outcome with significant cost reduction.

Sources indicate that while LLM context for app-related use cases as described in 1 and 2 are “restricted” to the app source code, for runtime management of apps on deployed infra, the underlying IT full stack comes into play. Here we define a knowledge graph (KG) encompassing entities (microservices, database/middleware services, MELT etc.) coupled with embedded (“tribal”) knowledge from domain experts. With such a graph and bounding the LLM to local bound reasoning for non-deterministic outcomes, an observability-driven approach is used to achieve reduced context space spanning the IT stack and underlying app source code (if relevant) for incident root cause analysis (and other use cases). With this approach, leveraging the equivalent Instana data model, we have seen the proprietary Instana “I3” (intelligent incident investigation [8]) agent achieve up to 4.0× improvement over ReAct agent with GPT-5.1 as measured using ITBench [9]. With Gemini 3 Flash the ReAct agent performance improves to within 17% lower than the I3 agent while consuming 1.6× more tokens, We have extended this approach to source code with agents for code analysis (leveraging program dependency graphs) and bug remediation (leveraging inference scaling), also tested on ITBench, illustrating superior performance for the source code analysis and bug remediation agents (Gemini 2.5 Flash) over state-of-the-art coding agent both for finding the culpable microservice (3.0×) and bug repair (1.6×) while consuming respectively 3.7× and 5.9× less tokens. This multi-agent system was unveiled at IBM Think as part of the newly unveiled IBM Concert Platform for shift-left IT Operations and is also being piloted internally with IBM CIO. [10].

According to recent reports, enterprises face increasingly complex and fragmented compliance requirements, forcing teams to spend considerable time manually creating controls, assessments and remediation plans. No centralized knowledge exists and fixes are written manually, which introduces a risk of errors and security gaps. Because compliance work is complex and multi-step, it requires coordinated policy-driven automation across specialized agents rather than manual effort or simple AI prompts. Our multi-agent system automates compliance by algorithmically decomposing complex tasks into coordinated steps, using adaptive planning, dynamic decomposition and workflow sequencing with continuous feedback to iteratively identify fixes and expand assessments. It is 1.3 – 2.0× more performant than prior agents (Claude 4 Sonnet) using fixed planning strategies, as also measured using ITBench. This approach transforms compliance into a continuously guided self-correcting process and dramatically improves outcomes, especially in complex scenarios, boosting success rates from single digits to as high as +80% (Claude 4 Sonnet). This multi-agent system and 16K+ digitized controls mappings were unveiled as part of IBM Sovereign Core at IBM Think, integrated with monitoring, drift detection, providing automated evidence generation, ensuring audit evidence stays securely within customer control. [12].

Industry observers note that the above examples illustrate the impact of agent logic in reducing LLM context and guiding the LLM to traverse the core of the workflow in a highly performant and cost-effective manner. Additionally, we have employed similar approaches to two case studies, one with a configurable generalist agent and runtime (CUGA) in the healthcare domain and another for the condition-based maintenance for physical assets with IBM Global Real Estate.

Recent findings suggest that case Study 1: Configurable Generalist Agent (CUGA) Healthcare benchmark - algorithmic policy enforcement. [13].

It has been revealed that the following health insurance customer care example is a compact illustration of why agentic systems outperform LLM-only conversational models in regulated environments. CUGA’s (configurable generalist agent) policy system implements policy-as-code for agent governance, which is enforced at runtime independent of model prompts and without fine-tuning. Our experiments show that the agent’s policy system closes large gaps in task correctness, enforcing structured workflows, safe intent handling, reliable tool usage, and controlled output formatting across all model families (Claude Opus – 4.5, GPT OSS 120B and GPT – 4.1) with accuracy improvements ranging from 15% to 26%. Authority is enforced through least-privilege disclosure, explicit compliance rules, and human escalation paths. Intelligent actions are proposed, while authority is exercised by policy and oversight mechanisms. Reasoning is autonomous; decision rights are constrained. CUGA is also a key component in the IBM Think Sovereign Core launch.

In a recent development, case Study 2: Condition-based Maintenance of Physical Assets for IBM Global Real Estate - directed acyclic graph. [14],[15].

Our recently released Maximo Condition Insights [16] agent analyzes large-scale asset data across thousands of assets and locations (sensors, work orders, failure modes and events analysis), using structured evidence and validation loops to reliably identify concerns, prioritize actions and support decision-making with consistent, traceable insights. We have piloted this agent (using GPT OSS 120B) internally with IBM Global Real Estate (GRE), reducing asset analysis time from 15-20 mins to 15-30 sec (a 97% improvement) and increasing asset review coverage from ~1% to ~30% spanning over 120 sites and 6K physical assets. Using AssetOpsBench, the Condition Insights agent reduced unsupported claims by 57%, cut verbosity by 35%, improved rule compliance by 30%, maintained near-zero contradictions, and lowered token usage by on average 77%, while slightly increasing diagnostic specificity. This agent, equipped with a directed acyclic graph, provides structural engineering and operational context to reduce unsupported reasoning under naive prompting, while constraint-aware prompting markedly improves rule adherence, reduces verbosity, and lowers overall token consumption without introducing instability.

Thesis builds brands on Bitcoin, backing its conviction with capital and code, and Studio Freight answers with a visual language pulled from indie hacker zines and early computing: black and white, gritty textures, hand-drawn spheres and gears, and one electric lime doing all the shouting. The asterisk sits at the center, somewhere between a footnote and a flag, and the whole identity reads like a samizdat pamphlet that learned to behave on a screen. The voice matches, what the studio calls adult punk: spirited defiance tempered with wisdom, unafraid to make guesses about restoring autonomy in tech.

In a recent development, two typefaces carry the system. Harber, a dot-gridded display face, holds the texture of a printout from a different internet, with dotted letterforms that spell the name at poster scale, in the site navigation, and ghosted behind the asterisk on the homepage. Antique Legacy Semibold does the clear work, setting plain statements in a voice that stays readable while the display type makes the noise.

Recent findings suggest that the grid is the dot grid itself. The asterisk mark, the dotted THESIS letterforms, and the dotted figures in the launch graphics all sit on the same dotted construction, so every panel reads as one argument. The studio coined a word for the position behind it, counterventure, naming a studio that creates ideas from the inside instead of waiting for them to walk in, operating against the extractive defaults of the venture model.

According to recent reports, the material language is print, even on screen. Hand-drawn spheres and gears, gritty textures, and a black-and-white field give the system the feel of print passed hand to hand, and the electric lime cuts through it in exactly one place at a time: a poster, a headline, a hand-drawn illustration on a lime field. The stationery keeps the same discipline, a white card that carries the name and the counterventure label, and nothing else.

Sources indicate that the system stretches across the launch site, where the asterisk fills a monitor above the tagline, and into product work, where a phone screen for tBTC carries the dot-grid mark and a line about decentralized cryptography. A poster fills its frame with one word in flat lime, and a manifesto sheet sets the studio's own words in typewriter type over the dotted asterisk, including its line about making bitcoin accessible to all.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads.
  • According to recent reports, in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks.
  • The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads. Mellum originally started as a code completion model. With Mellum2, we extend that foundation to a broader set of natural language and software engineering tasks while keeping the model focused on efficient inference and deployability. Modern AI systems increasingly rely on multiple model calls: routing, retrieval, summarization, planning, validation, and tool use. Many of these operations are latency-sensitive and do not require the largest available model. Mellum2 targets these workloads.

According to recent reports, in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks. Mellum2 is competitive with similarly sized open models while delivering more than 2x faster inference, making it suitable for high-throughput production workloads. Model architecture Mellum2 is a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token. This makes inference more efficient and helps reduce serving cost for real-time workloads. Mellum2 is intentionally focused on text and code rather than multimodal tasks. This specialization keeps the model compact and efficient for software engineering workloads.

Mellum2 works well as a lightweight routing and orchestration model in multi-model systems, including prompt classification, tool selection, and intermediate control-flow steps.

The model is well suited for latency-sensitive retrieval pipelines, including context compression, summarization, and retrieval post-processing.

Mellum2 can be used for agent subtasks such as planning, validation, transformation, and context preparation, reducing the need to invoke larger models for intermediate operations.

Because Mellum2 is open and efficient to serve, it can be deployed in self-hosted environments involving proprietary code or internal data.

As AI systems mature, the most effective architectures are becoming less monolithic. A single frontier model can be powerful, but production systems often need several specialized components working together: retrievers, routers, code-aware models, validators, tool callers, and larger reasoning models. We think of Mellum2 as a “focal” model: a fast, well-scoped model optimized for high-frequency tasks inside larger AI systems. The goal is not to replace every model in the stack. The goal is to make the stack faster, cheaper, and easier to control.

If you are building AI systems for software engineering – inside an IDE, in a RAG pipeline, as part of an agent workflow, or on private infrastructure – Mellum2 is ready to try.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years.
  • Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks reveals much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones revealed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model.
  • Customers want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks.
  • This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model. Adoption was immediate. Developers, enterprises, and partners started deploying Holo3 across a wide range of workflows, from browser automation and business software to internal tools and desktop applications. As adoption grew, we realized performance alone was no longer enough.

Customers want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks. They want deployment flexibility, from cloud inference to fully local execution on end-user devices.

This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family. Holo3.1 improves robustness across the three dimensions that matter most in production: environments (web, desktop, mobile), agent frameworks, and deployment targets. For the first time, we release quantized checkpoints optimized for local inference, including FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

Holo3.1 is a major step toward our vision of universal computer-use agents: systems that can operate across environments, integrate into any agent stack, and run wherever the workflow lives.

Based on the Qwen family, Holo3.1 was designed to improve robustness across the environments where computer-use agents are actually deployed, while retaining state-of-the-art performance.

As teams moved Holo3 from evaluation to production, we repeatedly observed the same challenge: strong performance in one setting does not necessarily transfer to another. Mobile devices, alternative agent harnesses, and different execution frameworks all introduce their own sources of distribution shift.

Recent findings suggest that holo3.1 expands Holo3's capabilities beyond browser and desktop control, delivering major gains on mobile environments. On AndroidWorld, our 35B-A3B model improves from 67% to 79.3%, while the smaller 4B and 9B variants improve from 58% to 72%.

To better support teams deploying Holo inside third-party agent stacks, Holo3.1 introduces native support for function-calling protocols in addition to the structured JSON outputs already available in Holo3.

Across OSWorld and our internal benchmark suite covering e-commerce, business software, and collaboration workflows, function-calling and native execution now achieve near-parity performance. Holo3.1 also delivers more than a 25% improvement over Holo3 when evaluated inside our Holotab product harness.

To further enable local and on-device inference, we are also releasing new model sizes including small models (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) for cost-effective and private deployment, in addition to the larger 35B-A3B model for state-of-the-art performance.

Performance versus cost for the Holo3.1 and Qwen 3.5 families. Overall performance averages the four H Corporate benchmarks first (so each family is equally weighted), then takes the mean across OSWorld, AndroidWorld, H Corporate, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

This is our first release to ship quantized weights. We’re starting with 35B-A3B checkpoints, available in FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

For NVFP4, we used NVIDIA's Model Optimizer in a W4A16 configuration. These checkpoints enable fast local inference for Computer Use Agents with little to no degradation in model performance. FP8 and NVFP4 achieve the same OSWorld scores, only about two points below the full-precision BF16 checkpoint.

The speedups are substantial: on DGX Spark, NVFP4 W4A16 delivers 1.41× the total token throughput of FP8 and 1.74× that of BF16.

We also release Q4 GGUF checkpoints aimed at local deployment of Computer Use Agents on consumer hardware.

The agent itself runs locally on a Windows or Mac machine, while the model can either run on that same machine—we include reference numbers for Apple Silicon—or on a DGX Spark on the same network. In both cases, execution stays fully private and local, with nothing leaving the user's network.

On Spark, agent harness optimizations we developed with NVIDIA combined with the NVFP4 quantization above deliver a compound ~2× end-to-end speedup over the FP8 baseline, cutting average step time from 6.8s to 3.3s.

Industry observers note that agent request rate across platforms and precisions. On DGX Spark, vLLM with NVFP4 achieves the highest request rate in both Default and Fast modes, followed by Q4 GGUF and FP8. These improvements and more will land in an upcoming desktop agent harness.

The Holo3.1 family is available in four sizes:.

We are also releasing optimized FP8, NVFP4, and Q4 GGUF checkpoints for local and edge deployment.

We look forward to seeing what developers build with Holo3.1.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Moon is now a few days past its First Quarter phase, and we're well into the Waxing Gibbous stage, which means each night, a little more of its surface is illuminated. This pattern will continue until we reach the Full Moon.

As of Friday, Nov. 20, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 77% of its surface visible.

It has been revealed that if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis and Tranquillitatis, as well as the Kepler Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Posidonius Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 14, and 17 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

According to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

Newly introduced Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

In a recent development, waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP. You can give your robot a newly introduced ability, like checking the weather or searching the web, by adding a Space from the Hub instead of editing the app. The tool keeps running in the Space itself, so no code is downloaded onto your machine. And you can publish your own tools for other people to use.

Adding a tool takes one command:.

Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.

Recent findings suggest that when you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable. The part we want to focus on here is the tools that make that possible. A tool is something the model can do during a conversation: play an emotion, move the head, look through the camera. Each tool has a name and a short description. The model reads those, decides when one is useful, calls it, and uses what comes back.

Today every tool is local and ships inside the app, and most of them are about the robot's body:.

A tool in the code isn't usable until it's enabled in a profile, a folder with two files that matter here: instructions.txt (the prompt) and tools.txt (the tools that are turned on).

The default profile enables the full set:.

If a name isn't in tools.txt, the model can't call it.

You can also write your own tool: add a Python file to the profile (or external_tools/), give it a name and description, and list that name in tools.txt.

Today there are built-in tools and custom local tools, and tools.txt decides which are active. This works well for the robot's body and keeps the trusted core small.

The constraint here is that every tool has to be local Python. For move_head or play_emotion that's right: they talk to the hardware and belong in the app but a lot of useful things have nothing to do with the body, like web search, weather, or lookups. For those, keeping everything local is mostly friction:.

Remote tools add a third kind, alongside the built-in and custom local tools you already have, for capabilities that are easier to publish, share, and enhancement on their own:.

We started with two canary tools, small test tools to exercise the newly introduced flow:.

They're enough to exercise the whole feature: install from the Hub, discover the remote tools, enable them per profile, and let the realtime backend call them exactly like built-in tools.

To use both at once, add each Space and their tools stack in the same profile:.

Now the robot can search the web and check the weather in the same conversation, which is exactly what the canary_web_search_weather profile below does.

Industry observers note that add validates the Space on the Hub, probes the MCP endpoint, discovers its tools, and by default appends the tool IDs to the active profile's tools.txt. The active profile is default unless you've set REACHY_MINI_CUSTOM_PROFILE. Use --install-only to skip that step.

tools.txt is the gatekeeper: a remote tool is only active if its ID appears in the profile's tools.txt, alongside whatever built-in tools you want.

Installed sources are persisted in:.

Each installed Space gets a local alias derived from its slug, with hyphens, dots, and slashes collapsing to underscores:.

Remote tools are then namespaced with a double underscore:.

This keeps remote tool names from colliding with built-in ones and lets multiple Spaces coexist in the same profile.

The implementation also strips redundant Space-name prefixes when possible, so a verbose remote tool name becomes a cleaner local ID. If stripping would cause a collision between two tools from the same Space, the code falls back to the fully namespaced name.

There is also a duplicate safety check at registry level: Tool.name values must be unique across the entire merged tool set. The app fails fast if two sources claim the same name.

For this work we created two focused canary profiles to isolate the MCP experiment from the full embodied tool set.

The first keeps a few expressive tools (emotions, head movement) and adds web search on top:.

The second is the same, plus the weather tool alongside search:.

The small physical tool set means Reachy Mini can still react expressively while answering current questions from the web.

In a recent development, the remote-tool plumbing gets the tools into the model. The prompts decide how the model uses them.

In a recent development, that was especially visible in the search-plus-weather canary. A combined question like:.

According to recent reports, can be handled in at least three ways: weather first then search, search first then weather, or both in the same turn. If the prompt is vague, the model serialises the calls and creates unnecessary latency. So the canary prompts became part of the feature, not just incidental configuration.

Two things are worth calling out. First, the Space has to actually behave like an MCP server; if tool discovery fails, the install fails. Second, prompt instructions can encourage parallel calls but cannot guarantee them. If deterministic orchestration matters for a use case, that logic should move from the prompt into code.

If you want others to use your tool, publish it as a public Gradio Space that exposes the standard MCP endpoint, and keep the tools stateless so they work well over the network. Whether a Space installs depends on this runtime behavior, not on tags.

Tags aren't required for installation, but they help people find compatible Spaces:.

Recent findings suggest that the app now has three kinds of tools sharing one registry: built-in, local custom, and remote MCP tools, and profiles still decide which of them a given assistant can reach. A small, trusted core stays at the center while the optional capabilities around it can be added, tested, and swapped without touching the app itself.

Industry observers note that what we're most curious about now is what people build. If you publish a tool Space, tag it reachy-mini-tool and mcp so others can find it. We'd love to see what Reachy Mini ends up able to do!

Acknowledgements: Many thanks to Fabien Danieau for proofreading this post and helping test the workflow, to Andres Marafioti for helping test it, and to Remi Fabre and the Pollen Robotics team for the ideas and feedback that shaped the remote tools workflow.

Great work on making Reachy even easier to customize!How can I add these MCP tools on a wireless Reachy Mini with a preinstalled conversation app?

The tools.txt approach makes the MCP integration especially clear. I like how remote tools are kept separate from the built-in robot tools while still being enabled per profile. The distinction between installing a Space and actually activating its tool IDs in tools.txt also seems vital, particularly when multiple remote tools are being used together.I’m also using an MCP server on my site, https://tinid.ph/, to work with AI agents, and it has been really useful for me. In particular, it has helped a lot with identifying and fixing technical issues on the site. The idea of keeping tools accessible to AI agents through MCP, rather than building every capability directly into the application, makes a lot of sense.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A unified customer profile (also called a single customer view) is one record that represents one real person, no matter which channel they used to reach you.
  • Without it, you get duplicate contacts, repeated questions ("What's your order number?" asked three times), and broadcasts that hit the same person on three channels.
  • Note: A unified profile is not a bigger contact table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A unified customer profile (also called a single customer view) is one record that represents one real person, no matter which channel they used to reach you. It combines their identities, conversation history, attributes, tags, and consent status into a single unified customer database entry.

Without it, you get duplicate contacts, repeated questions ("What's your order number?" asked three times), and broadcasts that hit the same person on three channels.

Note: A unified profile is not a bigger contact table. It is a graph: one person node connected to many channel identities.

The core problem is that every platform identifies people differently, and none of them hands you a universal ID.

Keep three concepts separate: the person, their channel identities, and the events that happen to them.

Tip: Store phone numbers in E.164 format (+8801XXXXXXXXX) from day one. Matching 017... against +8801... is a classic source of silent duplicates.

Identity resolution is the process of deciding that two identities belong to the same human. For messaging, keep it conservative: a wrong merge (two people combined) is much worse than a missed merge.

Only auto-merge when you have a verified shared key:.

When someone on Instagram or Telegram notes "my WhatsApp number is...", don't merge on the spot. Verify first:.

Industry observers note that warning: Never use display name alone as a matching key. "Ahmed Khan" is not a unique identifier.

With identities linked, the single customer view is one query:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the object your inbox, your automations, and your reports should all read from. Treat it as the single source of truth for unified customer data.

Most teams need to sync data to a CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, Zoho, or a custom one). Two rules keep it sane:.

Use idempotent upserts and a retry queue. Webhooks arrive twice, and CRMs rate-limit.

Sources indicate that once you have a unified profile, the best consumer of it is an AI agent that answers customers on any channel with full context. This is where AI tool calling (also called function calling in AI) comes in: the model doesn't query your database directly. It calls AI agent tools that you define, and you control what each tool can do.

Here is how AI agents use tools in this setup:.

In a recent development, good AI agent tool design is mostly about limiting blast radius. Following LLM function calling best practices:.

Sources indicate that notice there is no customer_id parameter. The server adds it. That one decision removes a whole class of tool calling in AI agents security problems.

Note: For anything that changes data (updating an email, requesting a link to another channel), use a separate write tool that triggers a confirmation step instead of acting immediately.

A single customer profile across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram comes down to a few decisions:.

If you'd rather not build all of this from scratch, platforms like Botsailor are built for omnichannel automation across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram, and are worth a look as a customer data solution if you want a unified inbox without owning the plumbing.
