Your Next Customer Is an AI Agent. Most Companies Still Aren't Ready to Be Evaluated by One.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A CAIO's perspective on GTM engineering, AI-native go-to-market and the agent-to-agent economy, where buyer AI agents shortlist vendors and only verifiable evidence gets you the meeting.
  • Your next customer may be an AI agent, one that evaluates 40 vendors overnight and books a human conversation only with the manufacturer that can prove its claims in a form a machine can verify.
  • Most commercial organizations were never designed for that kind of buyer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A CAIO's perspective on GTM engineering, AI-native go-to-market and the agent-to-agent economy, where buyer AI agents shortlist vendors and only verifiable evidence gets you the meeting. Originally published on my blog and LinkedIn.

Your next customer may be an AI agent, one that evaluates 40 vendors overnight and books a human conversation only with the manufacturer that can prove its claims in a form a machine can verify.

Most commercial organizations were never designed for that kind of buyer.

In a recent development, I've been thinking a lot about how AI is changing the way companies go to market. Most of the conversations I come across still circle familiar themes: AI-written sales emails, automated prospecting, smarter CRM systems, better seller productivity. All of that is useful. But I think it describes the small version of what is happening.

According to recent reports, the bigger shift begins when buyers start using AI agents not just to research products, but to shortlist vendors, compare solutions, test integrations and, eventually, negotiate within limits their company has approved. We have spent decades building sales and marketing organizations to influence human buying decisions. Very few of us have asked what changes when part of that decision is delegated to software.

That question is why GTM engineering has become so interesting to me. It is no longer only about automating how we sell. It is about how an enterprise makes itself discoverable, understandable, trustworthy and easy to buy from, for people and for the intelligent systems acting on their behalf. And that, in my view, is as much a technology architecture challenge as a sales challenge.

In a recent development, let me make this concrete. This is a hypothetical scenario, not a case study.

A manufacturer's procurement agent detects a latest requirement. Overnight, it screens 40 potential vendors on specifications, security evidence, integration fit and price, and narrows the list to three. It then contacts each vendor's own systems.

Two of them return well-designed but generic capability pages, the kind of content we have all been producing for years. The third returns a signed capability manifest, verified certifications, a sandbox already configured with the buyer's anonymized data, and documented outcomes from similar deployments.

The agent books a 20-minute call with a human, and only with the third vendor. That vendor's account executive joins the call already knowing the three open technical questions and exactly which evidence the agent relied on.

Figure 1: Who won the deal? A procurement agent screens 40 vendors and books a human call only with the vendor whose claims it can verify.

Notice what did not happen. There was no cold call, no lead moving through a funnel, and no salesperson controlling the flow of information. The firm that won was not the one with the largest sales team or the most polished marketing. It was the one whose products, knowledge and interfaces were ready to be evaluated by another intelligent system.

Sources indicate that I'm not predicting that enterprise procurement will be fully autonomous by 2028. Human buying committees will still make the significant decisions. But I believe this is the direction of travel, and it exposes a blind spot in how most of us have built our commercial organizations.

It helps to look at how we got here. Each generation of go-to-market solved the previous generation's bottleneck, and in doing so created a new one.

In the first generation, one account manager did nearly everything: found prospects, ran discovery, demonstrated the product, priced it, closed it and looked after the customer afterwards. Growth meant hiring more sellers. It worked until it didn't, because no single person can be excellent at a dozen different jobs.

The second generation broke that work into specialized roles (SDRs, account executives, customer success) connected by handoffs. Growth meant hiring more SDRs. That model is under strain today. Buyers do much more of their research on their own, they actively avoid vendors who send irrelevant outreach, and every handoff loses some context about the customer.

In a recent development, the third generation, which I think is just beginning, combines people and AI agents in a deliberately engineered system. Agents take on the repetitive, always-on work. People concentrate on strategy, trust and judgment. And a fresh discipline, GTM engineering, designs and continuously improves the system that connects them.

Figure 2: Three generations of go-to-market: the full-stack seller, the assembly line, and humans plus AI agents.

In a recent development, if prospecting, qualification and first-round discovery increasingly become software capabilities, it is reasonable to ask what the long-term economic case is for the traditional SDR-heavy model. I don't think the answer is "no humans." I think the answer is different humans doing different, more valuable work.

Sources indicate that the term "GTM engineer" has spread quickly, and I understand the skepticism. Plenty of people hear it and think of someone wiring enrichment tools to an email sequencer.

That is part of the job, but it misses the point. Traditional revenue operations focused on processes, systems, reporting and coordination. GTM engineering adds something new: the ability to build and continuously improve the technical systems through which a company finds, serves and grows its customers.

In practice, a capable GTM engineering function:.

Industry observers note that the strongest GTM engineers rarely start as pure software engineers. They tend to come from commercial roles: a seller or marketing-ops person who couldn't stop optimizing their own workflow. You cannot automate well what you have never done yourself.

According to recent reports, here is a simple example of the mindset. Imagine a customer who bought a product three months ago but has never completed the integration needed to get value from it. In a traditional model, someone in customer success might notice at the next quarterly review, if at all. A GTM engineering approach treats that as a signal worth designing for. The system detects the incomplete setup from product data, checks that it has the right customer and that nobody is already helping them, pulls the approved implementation guidance, and proposes help, not an upsell, to the account owner. Then it measures whether customers who received that help actually activated faster than similar customers who didn't.

Sources indicate that none of those steps is exotic on its own. What is fresh is treating the whole path, from signal to action to measured outcome, as a product that gets engineered, tested and improved over time.

This is the distinction I find most useful when talking with other executives.

AI-assisted GTM makes existing work faster. AI drafts outreach, summarizes meetings, enriches leads and recommends next steps. It is valuable, it is available today, and most organizations should be doing it.

AI-native GTM redesigns how the work happens. Intelligent systems coordinate discovery, evaluation, evidence, workflows and decisions, with people providing oversight where judgment and accountability matter.

The difference is not the technology. It is the ambition. AI-assisted GTM improves the efficiency of the existing commercial model. AI-native GTM questions whether that model is still the right one.

The evidence supports taking this seriously. Field studies of generative AI show strong gains on well-defined tasks and weaker (sometimes worse) judgment on tasks just beyond what the models handle reliably. And while executive surveys consistently find that most people feel personally more productive with AI, only a small share of companies report meaningful impact on profit. The ones that do tend to have one thing in common: they redesigned the workflow end to end rather than adding AI to the old one.

Renewals illustrate the difference well. An AI-assisted renewal process gives the account manager a better summary before the call: usage trends, open tickets, a suggested talking point. Useful, but the process is unchanged. An AI-native renewal process starts months earlier. It continuously watches whether the customer is realizing the value they bought, intervenes when adoption stalls, assembles evidence of outcomes as they happen, and brings a human in at the moments where a relationship conversation genuinely matters. By the time renewal arrives, the case has largely been made, by the customer's own results.

When I map out how commercial interactions are changing, I see three modes emerging side by side.

Figure 3: Commerce is splitting into three modes: human to human, human to agent, and agent to agent.

Recent findings suggest that the first is the one we know well: human to human, where trust, judgment and negotiation carry the day. The second is human to agent, where a buyer or seller uses AI to research, evaluate and act faster; clear, well-grounded answers win here. The third is agent to agent, where software on both sides handles discovery, evaluation and quoting. In that mode, verifiable evidence and trustworthy interfaces matter more than persuasion.

The third mode is where it gets genuinely upcoming, because the two agents represent competing interests. A buyer's agent is trying to optimize price, fit and risk. A seller's agent is trying to protect margin and make sure the customer is a good fit. That raises questions most GTM leaders have never had to answer. How do two agents that have never interacted establish trust? How does a seller verify what a buyer's agent is actually authorized to commit to? What prevents manipulation, whether through prompt injection or fabricated evidence? And at what point must the agents hand the conversation back to people?

As buyer-side agents mature, I expect them to negotiate standard terms within mandates their organizations have approved, escalating anything outside those limits to humans. That makes the traditional website only one of several front doors. Machine-readable product information, trusted APIs, verifiable evidence and agent-facing interfaces could become just as vital.

Picture what that front door looks like when the visitor is software. It is less a web page and more a trust gateway: it checks who the agent is and what it is allowed to commit to, serves only signed and current facts, and knows exactly when to hand the conversation to a person.

Figure 4: A trust gateway between a buyer's procurement agent and the seller's capability manifest, compliance proofs, pricing API, proof-of-value sandbox and seller agent.

Recent findings suggest that what would preparing for that look like in practice? I'd start with a few unglamorous questions:.

Sources indicate that most companies could improve on all four today, long before buyer agents become common. And every one of them also makes life easier for human buyers.

In autonomous commerce, authorization is not just a security checkbox. It becomes part of your brand.

In a recent development, one point for the technologists: protocols such as MCP are excellent for connecting AI to tools and data, but on their own they don't solve identity, authorization or negotiation between companies. That gap is where an important new layer of commercial infrastructure will be built.

According to recent reports, sophisticated AI models are becoming widely accessible. Every competitor can buy roughly the same ones. That raises the question I find most important: if intelligence is available to everyone, where does sustainable differentiation actually come from? I see three answers.

It has been revealed that context. I've become convinced that generating more content isn't the answer. Buyers are getting better at recognizing generic AI writing, and when you sound like everyone else, they assume you are like everyone else. What matters is whether your systems understand the customer's situation well enough to offer something genuinely useful, and that depends on proprietary context: your experts' perspective, your outcome data, your knowledge of why deals are won and lost.

This matters most at the top of the tech giant. In many growth-stage businesses, the founder's or CEO's point of view is the differentiation, and buyers are judging the leader as much as the product. The temptation is to let AI produce that voice at scale. I think that's backwards. The better pattern is to treat an executive's voice as infrastructure: capture their best emails, call recordings, talks and strong convictions, encode that into the context every outbound agent works from, and let AI scale and personalize it, not invent it. A weekly recorded conversation about customers, product and competitors can feed a month of content without the executive writing a word. Then, for the moments that really matter, a human adds back some "friction": a strong opinion, a specific story, an imperfect but genuine phrase. Perfectly polished prose slides past people. Texture gets read.

According to recent reports, done well, this is a loop rather than a campaign. The voice is captured and encoded once, agents scale it, people roughen it where it counts, and what lands feeds back into the next round.

Figure 5: The executive voice loop: capture, encode, generate, roughen, distribute and measure.

Evidence. A compelling story will still matter. But as AI participates in purchasing decisions, I expect verifiable evidence to carry more weight: specifications that can be checked, certifications that can be authenticated, pricing that is structured, benchmarks that can be reproduced. Brand credibility may come to depend as much on this evidence infrastructure as on messaging.

This is especially true when the product being sold is itself AI. Buyers of agentic products have good reasons to be cautious (accuracy, security, privacy, hallucinations) and a slide can't settle those concerns. They want to see the system working in their own context, over time. That shifts the emphasis from proof of concept ("does it work?") to proof of value ("does it create value here?"). I'd expect more vendors to reserve proofs of value for well-qualified buyers, charge for them, and treat them as the first phase of implementation rather than a throwaway demo, while making lighter self-service experiences, such as interactive product tours and sandboxes, available much earlier in the journey.

Industry observers note that learning. What interests me more than how quickly a company deploys agents is how well it learns from the outcomes. The question I keep coming back to is not "how many agents can we deploy?" but "how fast is our commercial system learning what actually creates customer value?".

I've started to think of this as a commercial learning rate: the time it takes to go from hypothesis to validated result, the share of experiments that actually change a decision, and how quickly you retire what isn't working. It is a metric I now care about more than most activity metrics. Models are rented; learning rate is owned.

One design choice makes the difference between compounding and chaos: what the system learns should reach production through an evaluated, authorized release, not by quietly drifting on its own.

Figure 6: Governed learning loop: act, observe, evaluate, learn and pass a release gate.

To make that concrete: suppose two competitors both launch AI-driven outreach to mid-market manufacturers. The first measures replies and meetings, sees the numbers rise, and scales. The second holds back a comparison group, tracks which meetings turn into qualified opportunities and healthy customers, and discovers within a few weeks that one segment converts well while another produces meetings that go nowhere. It shuts down the weak motion, doubles down on the strong one, and feeds what it learned into its targeting and messaging. Six months later, both companies are "using AI." Only one of them has become meaningfully smarter about its market.

In a recent development, that is why I'd rather see a team retire three experiments that didn't work than launch ten latest agents. The retirements are evidence that learning is happening.

Recent findings suggest that consider what happens when a customer's agent can reach your product specifications, technical documentation, service history and pricing directly. The CRM will still matter as the system of record. But the more strategic asset becomes the intelligence layer that decides what evidence supports a conclusion, what is likely to happen next, and which actions are permitted. For any CTO or CAIO, the question becomes: who owns that intelligence layer, your enterprise or your vendors?

These are the three principles I would put on the wall for any team building this:.

In a recent development, underneath, I find it useful to think in three planes. The execution plane is where AI interprets signals and acts for a specific customer, right now. The control plane is where software, not the model, decides what it may do: identity, permissions, approvals, budgets and a kill switch. The learning plane asks whether the action was right and worth it, and proposes improvements only through reviewed releases. AI interprets; software governs.

Figure 7: Execution, control and learning planes for AI-native GTM: AI interprets, software governs.

Two architectural choices deserve particular care.

The first is build versus buy. I'd buy the commodity pieces (enrichment, email delivery, standard connectors, workflow tooling) and keep control of what differentiates you: your customer definitions, your signal-to-action logic, your approved claims, your evaluation sets and your experiment history. If all of that lives inside a vendor's platform, your commercial learning walks out the door the day you switch.

In a recent development, the second is ownership across the leadership team. In my view this only works as a shared charter. The commercial leader owns customer outcomes and adoption. The CTO owns architecture, reliability and security. The CAIO owns the intelligence layer: which decisions AI should make, which models and tools are used, and the evaluation standard every system must meet. Without that clarity, GTM AI tends to become either a collection of disconnected sales tools or a slow central IT project. Neither works.

There's an aspect of this transformation that I don't think gets enough attention: what happens to the people who built their careers around these processes?

Consider a young sales development representative joining an enterprise technology tech giant. Traditionally, that person would spend months researching accounts, preparing for calls, hearing objections and slowly learning how buying decisions really get made. That apprenticeship is how many of today's best sales leaders, solution architects and consultants learned their craft.

Much of that work can now be assisted, or done outright, by AI. From a productivity standpoint, that is exciting. But it creates a harder question: if AI handles the research, qualification and preparation, where does the next generation develop its commercial instincts? Early data already suggests that hiring of young workers into AI-exposed roles is slowing.

In a recent development, I think we have to be careful not to confuse removing repetitive work with removing the experiences through which people develop judgment. And in commercial roles the stakes are higher than in many technical ones. When a commercial system makes a silent error, it doesn't stay inside the company. It lands on your customer. We need people who can tell when the system has misread a situation.

That means being much more intentional about how we develop talent: simulated customer conversations before real ones, rotations that put junior staff on the cases the AI got wrong or wasn't sure about, supervised time with real customers, and recognition for people who catch the system's mistakes rather than those who simply approve its output fastest.

The role of managers changes too. A sales manager who spent much of the week inspecting activity reports and pipeline hygiene will increasingly be coaching people on judgment: when to trust the system's recommendation, when to override it, and how to handle the customer situations it can't. That is a more demanding job, and most organizations haven't yet thought about how to prepare their managers for it.

And for individuals, the most durable career move I can see is to combine deep commercial understanding with the ability to shape, question and improve these systems. People who can do both will be the ones designing how their organizations grow.

Recent findings suggest that I also expect the shape of teams to change. The middle layer of routine coordination will likely thin out. Value will concentrate in two places: people who can design and govern these systems, and people who earn trust in complex, high-stakes relationships. The future of GTM isn't about fewer humans. It's about redefining where human expertise creates the most value, and continuing to develop it.

It has been revealed that the most practical way I've found to think about this is by jobs to be done rather than job titles. Agents are well suited to work that benefits from being available around the clock, multilingual, fast and consistent: administrative tasks, scheduling, routing, monitoring, and coordinating with other agents. People are better placed for strategy, customer meetings, negotiation, building alignment inside a buying group, and overseeing the agents themselves. The organizations that redesign roles around that split first, instead of simply bolting agents onto existing job descriptions, will set the cost and quality curve everyone else has to match.

Disruption is only half the story. Some of the biggest opportunities may come from infrastructure that enterprises don't yet realize they need. These are possibilities rather than proven categories, but they are the ones I'm watching:.

For professionals, the opportunity is just as real. Anyone who combines commercial experience with the ability to build, govern and evaluate these systems is going to be in demand for years.

According to recent reports, it's worth separating what is possible today from what is still emerging. Today, AI can reliably assist with research, drafting, summarization, enrichment and routing. Agents can take on well-bounded tasks inside clear rules. What is not yet reliable is long, multi-step commercial work without supervision: public benchmarks of agents on realistic CRM tasks show they still struggle as tasks get longer and more ambiguous. The gap is less about the models themselves and more about tool design, data, identity and evaluation.

Sources indicate that before choosing tools, I'd also choose where to aim. A common mistake is to start from the technology and look for somewhere to apply it, or to automate a process that was broken in the first place, paving the cowpath. A better starting point is the activity itself: how painful it is today, and how much a different outcome would be worth. I find three levels of ambition useful. You can optimize an activity, doing the same work faster or more cheaply. You can amplify it, using AI to produce outcomes that were previously uneconomic, like continuously refreshed competitive intelligence or a value model for every account. Or you can reinvent it, changing both how the work is done and what it delivers, as with an agent-run evaluation or a pipeline engine with no manual prospecting layer. Experiment in the first category to build skill; place your massive bets where pain and potential value are both highest. And give every cross-functional workflow a named owner, because the biggest gains usually sit between departments, not inside them.

I would also be cautious about giving commercial agents broad autonomy before we have confidence in their reliability, their decision boundaries and how they handle exceptions. Autonomy should be earned in stages:.

And measure what matters: incremental profit, how promptly customers get useful answers, the accuracy of what the system claims, and your commercial learning rate, not the number of agents deployed or emails sent.

Two risks are specific to putting an optimizing system in front of a market, and I think they deserve more attention than they get. The first is drift toward the wrong goal: a system rewarded for booked meetings or short-term conversion can quietly attract poorer-fit customers and hurt economics downstream. The second is a narrowing view of the market: a system that only acts on what has worked before stops exploring, and slowly loses sight of segments it never tried. Both are avoidable, by measuring lifecycle outcomes rather than activity, and by deliberately reserving some effort for exploration, but only if leaders know to look for them.

Sources indicate that predictions age badly, so treat these as hypotheses to test rather than forecasts. They're the ones I keep returning to.

Sources indicate that if even two of these come true, the companies best placed won't be the ones with the most AI tools. They'll be the ones that made themselves easy for machines to understand and safe for machines to trust.

Recent findings suggest that when I think about the future of GTM engineering, I don't see it as just another function inside sales or revenue operations. I see it becoming part of the enterprise's intelligence architecture: the way customer understanding, product capability, commercial decisions and AI-driven execution are connected into something that actually creates value.

According to recent reports, I don't believe anyone has all the answers yet. There are real open questions about trust, accountability, customer relationships and how much decision-making we should delegate to machines. But one thing is becoming clearer to me: deploying AI into existing commercial processes is only the beginning. The bigger opportunity is to rethink how those processes should work in the first place.

The next competitive advantage won't be the AI model. It will be the enterprise built around it.

So here is the question I'd put to every leadership team:.

Is your organization ready to be evaluated by a buyer's AI agent, or are you still optimizing only for human readers?

If you're working through this inside your own organization, I'd genuinely like to hear what you've found hardest.

GTM engineering is the discipline of building and continuously improving the technical systems through which a organization finds, serves and grows customers: the agents, data integrations, signal-to-action logic, escalation rules and evaluations behind go-to-market. Unlike traditional revenue operations, it treats the whole path from signal to action to measured outcome as a product.

AI-assisted GTM uses AI to make existing work faster, such as drafting outreach or summarizing meetings. AI-native GTM redesigns how the work happens, with intelligent systems coordinating discovery, evidence and decisions and people providing oversight where judgment and accountability matter.

It has been revealed that it is the emerging mode of commerce in which a buyer's AI agent and a seller's AI agent handle discovery, evaluation, quoting and, within approved mandates, negotiation. In this mode verifiable evidence and trustworthy, machine-readable interfaces matter more than persuasion.

Make product facts available in structured, current, approved form; make claims verifiable with owners and expiry dates; offer sandboxes and proof-of-value environments; and define explicitly what your own agents may promise on price, discounts and contract terms.

In a recent development, the intelligence layer: which decisions AI makes, which models and tools are used, and the evaluation standard every system must meet. The recommended architecture separates an execution plane, a control plane (identity, permissions, approvals, budgets, kill switch) and a learning plane, so that AI interprets and software governs.

The time it takes to go from a GTM hypothesis to a validated result, the share of experiments that change a decision, and how promptly underperforming motions are retired. It is a better measure of AI maturity than the number of agents deployed.

#57655. Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency.
  • Industry observers note that across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%.
  • Industry observers note that A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency. The paper benchmarked leading vision-language model families - both open-source and commercial - on a structured document extraction task: OCR on Brazilian Portuguese text. Among the reported metrics was text degeneration rate: the frequency with which a model produces a repetition loop instead of a transcription.

Industry observers note that across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%. Supervised fine-tuning reduced those rates for most models - but rarely to production-acceptable levels. The pattern points to a structural limitation: SFT optimizes for correct outputs, but does not explicitly penalize degeneration. There appears to be a ceiling on how much task-focused fine-tuning alone can reduce this failure mode (Text Degeneration Article).

Industry observers note that A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested. No exceptions. Average reduction: 59.4%. Best case: 87.6%.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

It has been revealed that that second stage was Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Almost all published DPO applications target chat alignment - models trained on human judgments about helpfulness or harmlessness (example: Rafailov et al., 2023). OCR carries none of that subjectivity: the task is objective, and there is no conversational context. There is, however, a clear preference signal. A correct transcription is chosen; a degeneration loop is rejected. DharmaOCR used that binary to construct a DPO training set, testing the technique not for alignment, but as a direct mitigation tool for a specific failure mode.

Recent findings suggest that the training signal came from the model itself - specifically from the outputs it produced when it failed. How a failure mode becomes a training signal is a structural question about the failure, not the model.

Why SFT has a ceiling on degeneration is still an open question - but the leading conjecture points to loss granularity. SFT trains token by token: each prediction is evaluated in isolation, and a repetition loop is never penalized as a completion-level failure. DPO inverts that logic. The training signal is the full output - chosen or rejected - which means a degenerated completion can be explicitly labeled as the wrong outcome, not just a sequence of locally probable tokens.

Industry observers note that when a training objective maximizes the likelihood of observed sequences, it concentrates probability mass in the regions of distribution space those sequences occupy. A model that enters one of those high-probability attractor regions during inference assigns elevated probability to the same token at the next step - which increases the probability further, which sustains the loop until the sequence hits the maximum token limit. Text degeneration is the output of this geometry: a self-reinforcing repetition loop that an autoregressive model cannot exit without external intervention (Holtzman et al., 2020). It is not purely a decoding artifact. The attractor involves the training objective, the learned distribution, and how probability mass concentrates during inference - a systems-level failure rather than a failure localized to any single component.

The geometry of this failure is visible at the token level.

Figure 2: When a token dominates its own conditional distribution, every sampling step deepens the attractor. The decoder samples from this geometry; it does not determine it.

Industry observers note that inference-layer interventions - repetition penalties, temperature adjustments, early-abort logic - operate on the sampling step. They contain the symptom without touching the distribution that produces it. The attractor persists.

Supervised fine-tuning moves the distribution closer to the task domain. For a structured generation pipeline, this means training on domain-specific documents, in the target language, with the required output format. The model gains fluency with longer sequences, constrained syntax, domain vocabulary. What SFT does not do is attack degeneration directly. Its objective - maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences - has no term that penalizes repetition loops. The failure mode is simply outside the scope of what the training signal optimizes for.

One model family in the DharmaOCR benchmark revealed an unexpected pattern: vanilla degeneration rate of 0.60%, rising to 3.23% after SFT, before a subsequent DPO stage brought it to 1.41%. It is a single data point - an exception, not a rule - and it would be overstating the evidence to treat it as proof of a mechanism. What it does illustrate is that SFT does not reliably reduce degeneration. Capability and degeneration resistance can move independently.

The distinction matters structurally. SFT and DPO are not interchangeable training stages performing the same operation at different intensities. SFT closes the distance between the model's prior distribution and the task domain. What it does not do is target degeneration as an objective - its effect on the failure mode is incidental, and the benchmark results show it is not consistent. The attractor that produces degeneration is not a problem with the model's proximity to the task - it is a problem with the shape of the distribution space the model now occupies.

According to recent reports, addressing that geometry requires a training signal built specifically to point the model away from its own failure modes. For a structured, non-conversational task with no human preference labels and no conventional "helpful versus harmful" distinction, constructing that signal is a design decision.

The DharmaOCR pipeline's contribution to DPO methodology is specific: it used the SFT model's own degenerate outputs as the rejected examples - not as noise to remove, but as the negative training signal the optimization needed.

DPO requires preference pairs: a chosen output and a rejected output for the same input, with a quality difference clear enough for the optimization to learn from. In chat alignment, human annotators produce those judgments - rating responses as more or less helpful, accurate, or safe. Structured generation tasks have no equivalent annotation source. An OCR pipeline either produces a correct transcription or it does not. Quality differences exist, but they are not produced by human preference rankings - they are produced by the task's own criteria for correctness.

Industry observers note that the DharmaOCR pipeline identified a preference signal that structured generation tasks already produce: the range of outputs the SFT model generates in inference. A model capable of performing a structured task is also capable of failing at it in characteristic ways. Those failures - outputs that enter the degeneration attractor - are not noise to filter. They are the most informative negative signal available.

The paper implemented this on 23,726 training documents, generating multiple candidate responses per document with the SFT model and scoring each with an automated LLM judge. The pipeline is shown below.

Figure 3: The critical design decision is not in the pipeline's structure - it is in what the pipeline preserved: outputs displaying text degeneration were deliberately labeled as rejected examples, not filtered out as low-quality noise.

The conventional response when degenerate outputs appear in training data is to remove them. They are low-quality signal; filtering produces a cleaner dataset. The DharmaOCR approach inverted this logic. Degenerate outputs were deliberately retained as the rejected examples in each (chosen, rejected) pair, because they represent exactly the failure mode the DPO stage was designed to suppress. Removing them would have discarded the clearest target available.

In a recent development, the paper describes this as "preference-guided implicit unlikelihood" - the model is trained not only toward better outputs but away from a specific class of failure. Where SFT maximizes the likelihood of high-quality outputs, the DPO stage simultaneously penalizes outputs displaying the degeneration attractor geometry. The direction of the optimization is explicit in a way SFT alone cannot achieve.

Degenerate outputs are particularly well-suited as rejection examples because they represent a consistent failure mode rather than varied low-quality outputs. A transcription that misses words is low quality, but its failure is case-specific. Repetition loops, by contrast, appeared persistently across documents and model families even after SFT - a pattern consistent with a failure mode that likelihood-based optimization does not reliably correct. DPO applies its loss differently: at the completion level, with explicit rejection signals. The post-hoc analysis cannot establish causality, but the evidence suggests that what SFT's objective leaves unresolved, DPO's may address.

Sources indicate that this approach requires no specialized annotation infrastructure - only a model capable of producing both acceptable and identifiable-failure outputs, and a scoring model to label preference pairs. A rule-based mechanism could detect repetition loops mechanically - but it could not identify which outputs represented high-quality transcriptions worth preserving as chosen examples.

In a recent development, the scoring model does both: it flags degeneration as the rejected output and validates clean extractions as the chosen one, keeping the model's extraction capability intact while the DPO signal penalizes the failure mode. Whether the resulting training signal successfully moves the distribution in the intended direction - and whether it does so consistently across architectures - is the evidence question.

The DPO stage reduced text degeneration in every model family tested - with reductions ranging from 37% to 88% and an average of 59.4% relative to SFT alone. The result held across architectures, parameter scales, and starting degeneration profiles that differed by more than one order of magnitude. One case in the dataset saw degeneration increase after the SFT stage before DPO corrected it. That case does not complicate the consistency. It confirms the mechanism more directly than any of the others.

In a recent development, figure 1 reveals the three-stage degeneration rate for each of the five model families tested: Vanilla, SFT, and SFT+DPO. In four of the five families, degeneration falls at each stage. The fifth family's bars move differently - and that difference is the most analytically important data point in the study.

Sources indicate that the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result, read carefully, is not a complication. It is a confirmation. The model's vanilla degeneration rate was 0.60% - not because it was stable, but because it was too generic to produce long structured outputs at all. The model was not entering the degeneration attractor because it was not attempting the task seriously enough to find it.

SFT changed that. After domain adaptation, Qwen2.5-VL-3B became capable of the task - producing longer, more structured outputs with the domain vocabulary and format the pipeline required. That capability brought it into proximity with the degeneration attractor for the first time. Its degeneration rate rose to 3.23%.

This is the mechanism made empirically visible: SFT moved the model toward the task and toward the task's failure geometry simultaneously. These are not necessarily the same operation. A training stage that increases task capability can increase failure-mode exposure as a side effect - particularly when the failure mode lives at the edge of the capability frontier. Treated as the same operation, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result looks like an error. Treated as distinct operations - which is what the SFT + DPO pipeline formally does - the result is consistent with the hypothesis that SFT and DPO address different failure dimensions.

It has been revealed that the DPO stage then brought the degeneration rate to 1.41%. It did not restore the vanilla baseline because it was not designed to: the model after SFT was more capable than it had been, and a return to 0.60% would have required undoing that capability. What the DPO stage did was address the failure geometry the SFT stage had introduced.

The remaining four model families add quantitative weight to the same conclusion. Figure 1 demonstrates the SFT-to-SFT+DPO comparison for all five.

It has been revealed that figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

No model family showed degeneration increasing after DPO. No family was immune to its effect. The consistency extends to gemma-3–4b-it, which entered the benchmark with the highest vanilla degeneration rate by an order of magnitude - 33.96%, compared to the next highest at 2.62% - and still reached a 75% reduction after the DPO stage. The reduction range - 37.3% to 87.6% - reflects differences in starting configuration and architecture, not inconsistency in the intervention's direction.

In a recent development, this is not a proof of universal applicability. DPO may not transfer to every domain, failure mode, or model family. What the DharmaOCR benchmark provides is evidence across five OCR architectures that the core hypothesis holds: optimizing over complete preference pairs - rather than maximizing token-level likelihood - addresses a failure mode that SFT structurally cannot target. The result was consistent in direction across every model family tested. That consistency, within the scope of this benchmark, is what the evidence supports.

The DharmaOCR approach was possible because this pipeline satisfied a set of structural conditions that allowed a DPO training stage to function as designed - conditions whose presence or absence determines whether the same methodology applies elsewhere (Dharma OCR Paper on ArXiv). It was not possible because OCR is a unique domain.

According to recent reports, the first condition is that the failure mode be identifiable as a distinct class of output, not just a point on a quality continuum. Text degeneration qualifies because a repetition loop is categorically different from a transcription that misses words or misreads a character. The output is not merely suboptimal - it is broken in a specific, behaviorally recognizable way. That categorical distinctness is what allowed the pipeline to construct preference pairs where the rejected examples represented a coherent failure geometry, not noise. A task whose failure modes blend into its range of acceptable variation lacks this property.

The second condition is that a scoring mechanism can reliably distinguish acceptable outputs from failure-mode outputs without requiring human annotation. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, an automated LLM judge scored candidate responses against four task-specific criteria. The scoring did not need to be perfect - it needed to be consistent enough to produce preference pairs with a meaningful quality gap between chosen and rejected. Pairs with ambiguous quality differences contribute noise to DPO training, not signal. The judge's consistency was a design requirement, not an incidental feature.

The third condition is sufficient volume - enough inference outputs to generate a preference dataset with meaningful variance in quality. This is not an extraordinary requirement by fine-tuning standards, but it is a real one.

It has been revealed that when all three conditions are present, the methodological move is structurally available. The design decision at the center of the DharmaOCR pipeline - treating the model's own failure outputs as the rejected examples rather than filtering them - applies wherever a model's failures are categorically identifiable, scoreable, and sufficiently numerous.

Sources indicate that the practical implication for ML engineers building structured generation pipelines is direct. SFT is necessary - it closes the distance between a generalist model and a task-capable one. It is not sufficient for structured output reliability, because task capability and degeneration resistance are different properties of the distribution. A DPO stage after SFT is a one-time training investment. In the DharmaOCR results, the degeneration reduction did not come at the cost of extraction quality - the paper's benchmark results show both moving together (Specialization Beats Scale article).

Recent findings suggest that what makes a failure mode usable as training signal is not the domain - it is whether the failures are consistent enough, identifiable enough, and numerous enough to constitute a legible signal. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, they were. Whether the same holds in another context is a structural question about the task's failure mode, not a question about the model family or the domain.

The DharmaOCR result does not depend on the domain being special. It depends on the failures being useful.

Sources indicate that text degeneration qualifies as useful because it is categorically distinct from acceptable outputs, consistently produced across inference runs, and reliably scoreable without human annotation. Those three properties - not the OCR context, not the model family, not the language - determined whether the preference dataset was tractable. A failure mode that satisfies them is not noise to remove. It is the most direct evidence available of where the distribution should not go.

The DPO stage used that evidence. Degeneration fell in every model family tested - in models that entered the benchmark with vanilla rates below 1% and in models that entered with rates above 33%. The direction held. The pipeline did not discard its failures. It trained on them.

It has been revealed that interesting explanation of how Direct Preference Optimization can improve model alignment beyond traditional chatbot applications. I think techniques like this are crucial for making AI systems more reliable and better at understanding user intent. This is particularly relevant when building a customer service chatbot, where accurate, relevant, and helpful responses can make a big difference in the user experience. Consistency and understanding context are just as important as generating natural-sounding answers. I recently came across this article that shares some useful insights into how businesses can use AI chatbots to improve customer service: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-chatbot-for-customer-service. It adds another useful perspective to the discussion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BOND builds the Aleph Farms brand identity from a single flipped letter for cultivated meat: the ancient aleph, turned over, becomes an ox.

BOND calls it turning steak on its head. Cultivated meat is one of the most significant developments in food production in generations, and the studio treats it as a story about continuity, not the future. Aleph Farms grows meat directly from animal cells, without raising or slaughtering animals, and BOND was asked to build both the parent brand and its first consumer product brand, Aleph Cuts. The name comes from the first letter of one of humanity's oldest writing systems, first drawn as the pictogram of an ox, and the identity took Gold at the European Design Awards in 2024.

It has been revealed that the wordmark does the talking. Aleph Farms reads in a sturdy grotesque, white on a deep green field, with the flipped letter tucked into a circle as the mark, the ox reappearing as a small geometric head. Aleph Cuts gets a different voice entirely: soft, rounded, almost liquid letterforms in dark green on coral, the same ox mark sitting beside it. The parent brand is the steady statement, the product brand is the appetite.

Industry observers note that the flip is the organising principle of the whole system. BOND runs it through typography, motion, imagery, and communication, so every panel reads as one argument. The palette stays tight: deep green, coral, and pale blue against off-white, with the ox mark repeating at every scale, from card to plate. The parent brand and the product brand keep distinct roles while sharing the same idea and visual language.

The material language is quiet and tactile. Business cards carry the mark blind debossed into dark green and white stock, the circle and the ox pressed into the paper rather than printed on it. The same mark is pressed into the center of a plate, a small stamped seal in the middle of an empty dish, waiting for the food. Nothing shouts. The identity holds its nerve and lets the mark do the work.

Julia Stotz photographs the food the way the brand thinks. A skewer comes off a smoking grill against a dark green backdrop, sliced steak stacks on a white plate with mushrooms and peppers, and the meat stays the subject, never a prop. The photography keeps the palette of the system, green backdrops, pale cloth, so the product shots sit inside the identity, not next to it. The result is a brand for something that never existed before that still looks like it has always been at the table.

Does GTA 6 Use AI? Take-Two and Claude Code

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I run a small consultancy that builds Atlassian apps and AI tooling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Does Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 use AI? Not generative AI, claims its publisher. Nothing we found contradicts that, but the denial covers generative AI in this one game. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz in February that generative AI "has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building". In the same breath he noted the company's products "have always been built with machine learning and artificial intelligence". Take-Two's own annual reports used the phrase "artificial intelligence" 0 times from fiscal 2015 to 2023 and 7 times in fiscal 2026, by our count of twelve filings. Claude Code is Anthropic's AI coding agent, and it can also control a computer's screen. A viral post says it finished the game in twelve hours. The post comes from a seven-week-old account with no log, about a game that is not on PC.

Grand Theft Auto VI (the sixth main game, GTA 6 for short) came out on 19 November 2026 on PlayStation 5 (PS5) and Xbox Series X|S. On launch day its English Wikipedia page had 750,227 views, more than any other article that day (only the Main Page and the search page ranked higher). On 10 November it had 64,375.

I run a small consultancy that builds Atlassian apps and AI tooling. So I care less about the game than about how a publisher this size talks about AI to investors, in documents its lawyers sign. I read twelve of Take-Two's annual reports and three of its patents, and then I traced the viral post back to its source. A lot of it applies to any team putting AI into its own work.

Industry observers note that the question mixes up three things. The answers differ.

The main source is Zelnick's interview with GamesIndustry.biz, published on 3 February 2026:.

"Specifically with regards to GTA 6, Generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That's what differentiates them. They're built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood. They're not procedurally generated, they shouldn't be.".

According to recent reports, the denial starts with a qualifier. So it covers one game. The timing matters too. GamesIndustry.biz notes the interview came after a week in which Take-Two's stock fell to an 11-month low following Google's announcement of Project Genie, which GamesIndustry.biz calls an experimental AI "playable world" tool. On the earnings call the same day, Take-Two president Karl Slatoff said Genie "is not a game engine". To him it looked "more like a procedurally generated interactive video at this point" (transcript).

Rockstar's own answer came second-hand. IGN reported in August 2026 that Kinda Funny's Greg Miller asked Rockstar "point-blank" about generative AI in GTA 6. The team told him there is "no AI" used in the game. That is a journalist's account of a verbal answer at a preview event, and I found no written Rockstar statement saying the same.

In a recent development, the same interview has the line most headlines skipped: "This company's products have always been built with machine learning and artificial intelligence ... right now we have hundreds of pilots and implementations across our company, including within our studios. And we're already seeing instances where generative AI tools are driving costs and time efficiencies." On the earnings call he said generative AI "is already moving into the category of efficiency".

So the company's line is simple: AI goes into the tools that build the game, and the game itself, the streets and the people in them, is made by hand. It never names the tools. It never indicates whether Rockstar is one of the studios running pilots either, and I found nothing public that does.

Recent findings suggest that the voice actors are part of the same picture. The Screen Actors Guild (SAG) and the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA) merged into one US actors' union, SAG-AFTRA. It struck video game makers in 2024-25 over "fair compensation and the right of informed consent for the AI use" of performers. A rule from an older agreement exempted games that started production more than a year before the strike, and GTA VI was one of them. The union's chief contracts officer, Ray Rodriguez, called that legacy rule "insane, but it's there" (PC Gamer). The deal that ended the 320-day strike passed with 95.04% of votes and requires consent and disclosure for digital replicas (TheWrap). No source indicates which agreement GTA VI's performers worked under.

I think upscaling is the most concrete answer to the question. It is the one place a neural network is publicly known to touch the game, the step that turns a lower-resolution frame into a sharper one. On PS5 Pro, Rockstar notes it uses Sony's PSSR (short for PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) in its second version, PSSR2 (as Rockstar writes it), to upscale 1440p to 4K. Sony's Mark Cerny describes it as "an AI library that analyzes game images pixel by pixel", built with AMD (the chipmaker behind the console's processor). Digital Foundry's tests, as reported by Dexerto, found the PSSR output on the Pro "convincingly passes for native 4K".

According to recent reports, rockstar's technology leads stated in a statement to Wccftech that the Xbox Series S version starts at 720p and reaches 1080p "using AMD FSR Upscaling 4". FSR, short for FidelityFX Super Resolution, is AMD's upscaler. AMD calls it "ML-based FSR Upscaling" (ML, short for machine learning) and says FSR 4 is its earlier name. On PS5 and Series X, Rockstar upscales 1440p to 4K with its own TAA (temporal anti-aliasing) upscaler, which it calls its "in-house TAA solution". It does not mention machine learning for that one.

Interviews are what a CEO wants you to hear. A 10-K is the annual report a US-listed manufacturer files with the SEC (the US Securities and Exchange Commission). Its risk factors section lists what the company's lawyers think could hurt the business. So we downloaded twelve of them from EDGAR, the SEC's filing database, for fiscal 2015 to fiscal 2026. Take-Two's fiscal year ends on 31 March. A 20-line Python script strips the HTML and counts the terms. The part that matters is the patterns:.

The other three patterns ignore case.

It has been revealed that the jump came in 2024, but the nine reports with no mention at all say more to me than the seven mentions in 2026: until fiscal 2024, Take-Two did not name AI to investors anywhere in its annual report. The reports stay between 51,874 and 71,076 words. Length did not drive the count. And the term was not always absent. EDGAR's full-text search finds "artificial intelligence" in two much older Take-Two reports, for fiscal 2005 and 2006. There, "expanded artificial intelligence capabilities of new platforms" is one of the things that would make people buy new consoles. About twenty years ago AI was a selling point of the hardware. From fiscal 2024 it sits mainly in the risk factors, and the count has grown every year since.

I'd put this sentence in front of any team rolling out AI assistants, in games or anywhere else, because I think it names the likeliest way an AI tool ends up hurting a organization:.

"our employees, contractors, vendors, or other partners may use AI tools in ways that are inconsistent with our policies or expectations, including by entering confidential, proprietary, personal, or regulated information into third-party AI services, and some AI providers may have limited operating histories or governance processes".

The same filing states Take-Two is "investing in artificial intelligence ("AI") tools and technologies" to "enhance game play". So the 2026 report holds both positions at once: invest in AI, and warn that your own people may leak data into it. A risk factor says what "may" happen. This sentence reports no incident.

Recent findings suggest that search "gta 6 ai npc patent" and you get fan theories. Each NPC (non-player character, one of the people in the street) is where game AI lives. Here is what is on the record.

In a recent development, edge's cover story, quoted by PC Gamer, says Rockstar set up a Los Angeles team of writers and directors for its crowds. The studio "art-directed every [NPC], creating around 600,000 animations". Each pedestrian gets personality traits that help decide how it reacts: temperament, aggression, where it is, what it has seen and how you treated it. That reads like classic, hand-authored game AI. No source says how the traits work. Nobody says whether any of it is trained.

Industry observers note that the patents are Take-Two's. I read their claims (the numbered parts that say what a patent protects).

US11620781B1, "System and method for virtual character locomotion", was filed on 23 October 2020 and granted on 4 April 2023. Claim 1 describes "motion animation blocks" and "archetype blocks" that are "functionally independent from the core game logic". Claim 7 claims the blocks can be defined in XML meta files. I searched the page text for "machine learning", "neural network" and "trained model": 0 hits.

US11071916B2, "System and method for virtual navigation in a gaming environment", was filed on 24 April 2019 and granted on 27 July 2021. It builds a coarse graph from the detailed road network and looks a route on it, so the game loads fewer detailed nodes. US11684855B2 is a later patent on the same navigation idea, granted on 27 June 2023.

None of them names GTA VI or any other game. I don't think they prove anything about it. Kotaku described the locomotion patent's first-listed inventor, Tobias Kleanthous, as a former Rockstar lead AI and gameplay programmer, and said it had asked Rockstar for comment. The article prints no reply.

Two months after the "zero part" interview, Game Developer reported on 3 April 2026 that Take-Two had laid off its head of AI, Luke Dicken (in the role since January 2025), and at least four others from the AI team. Take-Two declined to comment. So the "hundreds of pilots" interview and the end of its central AI team are two months apart, and I can't tell how the two fit. I checked the 10-K for that fiscal year, filed seven weeks after the layoff report, and none of its AI sentences mentions the team or the cuts.

Ten days before launch, on the 9 November call, an analyst asked about AI-assisted reverse engineering and decompilation of games. Zelnick remarked "it's going to become more of a challenge" and that the manufacturer is "utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities" (transcript). Rockstar has paid for leaks before: it said the 2022 hack that leaked unfinished GTA VI footage cost $5 million to recover from, plus thousands of hours of staff time (BBC).

In a recent development, on 19 November, launch day, the X account @⁠0xGoldTooth posted "Claude Code just finished GTA 6 in 12 hours while I was at work". The post says it "learned the controls in 15 minutes" and went "through the game files on its own". GameGPU wrote it up as news. The post had 3,763,124 views when we read it on 21 November.

Then there is the tool itself. Computer use is the Claude feature that looks at the screen and clicks and types. Anthropic's docs call it a research preview: in the Claude Code CLI it runs only on macOS, and the Desktop app adds Windows. Computer use "is the broadest and slowest" way for Claude to act, so it tries more precise tools first. Every screenshot is downscaled before the model sees it (a 3456×2234 screen goes to about 1372×887). Sony's Remote Play does stream a PS5 to a Mac, but Sony lists a DualSense controller among the things you need to play, and its on-screen panel only gives the PlayStation, Create and Options buttons, while computer use clicks and types. Once connected, Sony indicates, "the screen of your PS5 console displays on your Mac". Nothing on that page lets the Mac open the console's files. Tom's Hardware notes that PC players can stream the game through Xbox Cloud Gaming. The post does not say it used either service. The claim is a twelve-hour finish of a game rated 99 on Metacritic plus a trawl through "the game files", from a fresh account. I found no log anywhere. I would not repeat it as news, and I'm surprised GameGPU did.

The documented Claude-and-GTA story is smaller and more useful. In June, Gizmodo covered Ziwen Xu, a 25-year-old founder who tried to build a GTA-style game by prompting an AI agent instead of coding it himself. He upgraded to Claude Max 20x, an Anthropic subscription, to "beat the real GTA 6 to launch". On day two he wrote that the agent built downtown Los Angeles skyscrapers, "which is a problem, because this is supposed to be Florida". He had also burned 33% of his weekly usage in one day. If you want measured numbers on what these agents finish, our agentic coding benchmark results are where we keep them.

Industry observers note that take-Two split AI use in two: tools that make the work faster, and content that ships to the customer. Valve drew the same line on Steam. Valve's disclosure rules ask about "Pre-Generated" content made with AI during development and "Live-Generated" content made while the game runs. The January 2026 patch says "efficiency gains through the use of these tools is not the focus". Activision's Steam page for Call of Duty is an example of a Pre-Generated disclosure: "Our team uses generative AI tools to help develop some in game assets.".

Recent findings suggest that I think it's the right split, and it works as a policy for a software team too. AI that drafts the Jira ticket, summarises the Confluence page or writes the first version of a test is a tooling decision, while AI output that reaches a customer (release notes, a support answer, code in the product) needs the review and disclosure you would want from a contractor. Write the two lists down. Keep them separate and most of the arguments go away.

The people side is not settled, even in games. GDC's 2026 State of the Game Industry asked more than 2,300 professionals. 52% think generative AI is hurting the industry, up from 18% two years earlier. Still, 36% use it at work. 30% of respondents at game studios use AI tools, against 58% at publishers, support teams and marketing firms.

And the 10-K's data-leak sentence applies just as much to a Jira or Confluence site. Before arguing about whether an AI feature is allowed, check what your initiative lets you switch off. I'd start there. We wrote up which Atlassian prepares let you opt out of AI training and what stays on when you disable Rovo.

Sources indicate that still unknown: whether any of GTA VI's characters, animation or physics use a trained model, which AI tools Rockstar's own developers use, and whether the patents shipped. Rockstar may answer some of it in a technical talk one day. Has your team written down which of its AI uses are tooling and which ship to customers?

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.
