#57651. Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2208 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our consumers over the years.
  • Sources indicate that we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

Recent findings suggest that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our consumers over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

Sources indicate that we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

Recent findings suggest that the bars count distinct consumers per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

Industry observers note that humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

Recent findings suggest that when hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:.

A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

In practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but owners can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:.

For a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:.

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

Recent findings suggest that hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that shows exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:.

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):.

In a recent development, the command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

According to recent reports, to find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

In a recent development, (self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub said otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.).

Sources indicate that we defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:.

We run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

In a recent development, the config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

Industry observers note that the two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:.

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

The second image indicates token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:.

On a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

Industry observers note that hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:.

Recent findings suggest that what does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:.

It has been revealed that on both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

Sources indicate that we benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:.

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:.

Then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:.

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

Sources indicate that building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

Giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The crucial part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

#57650. React `taint` APIs in 2026: Preventing Sensitive Data From Accidentally Reaching Client Components

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2316 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

React `taint` APIs in 2026: Preventing Sensitive Data From Accidentally Reaching Client Components

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.
  • React Server Components introduced a split between server and client code that eliminated entire classes of security vulnerabilities.
  • Problem diagram showing tainted API key passed to client component causing silent data exposure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

React Server Components introduced a split between server and client code that eliminated entire classes of security vulnerabilities. Developers no longer ship database credentials or API keys to browsers because server-side logic stays on the server. The architecture itself prevents the mistake. But React 19.3 added two experimental APIs that solve a different problem: when server-side values accidentally cross into client components through serialization. The experimental_taintUniqueValue and experimental_taintObjectReference functions mark values as unsafe for client use, and React throws an error at build time or runtime if those values reach a component boundary. This prevents an entire category of data exposure that authentication checks and input validation cannot catch.

Problem diagram showing tainted API key passed to client component causing silent data exposure.

Taint APIs address the gap between server logic and client rendering. A Server Action might authenticate consumers correctly and validate every input, but if it returns an object containing internal fields or configuration values, those fields serialize and reach the browser. The taint APIs mark specific values as forbidden, and React enforces that boundary automatically.

Solution diagram showing tainted API key blocked by React before reaching client.

Sources indicate that react provides two taint functions that mark values as unsafe for client use. Both functions throw an error when React attempts to serialize the marked value and send it to a client component. The experimental_taintUniqueValue function blocks primitive values like strings and numbers, while experimental_taintObjectReference blocks entire objects from crossing the server-client boundary.

Sources indicate that the runtime behavior differs between development and production. In development mode, React throws an error immediately when a tainted value reaches a client component boundary. In production builds with Server Components enabled, React logs the error and prevents serialization but does not crash the application. This matches the progressive enhancement philosophy where server-side failures degrade gracefully.

Taint API hierarchy showing how unique values and object references block different data types.

Industry observers note that the taint functions accept a message parameter that React displays when the error occurs. This message should identify what failed and where the developer should look. Generic messages like "sensitive data" provide no actionable information during debugging. Specific messages like "SERVICE_API_KEY from systemConfig leaked to client component" point directly to the source.

Tainting happens at the value level, not the variable level. Reassigning a tainted value to a new variable does not remove the taint. React tracks the actual data, so passing const newKey = apiKey and then passing newKey to a client component still triggers the error. The taint follows the value through any number of assignments.

Derived values remain untainted by default unless they contain the original tainted data. If code hashes a tainted API key, the hash is a new value and React allows it to serialize. If code creates a substring of a tainted value, that substring inherits the taint. The distinction matters for logging, analytics, and masked display values that derive from sensitive sources.

The taint APIs integrate with Server Actions and Server Functions automatically. Any value returned from a Server Action that gets marked with a taint function will block serialization before React sends the response to the client. This prevents an entire class of mistakes where developers return raw database rows or configuration objects that contain sensitive fields mixed with safe fields.

Sources indicate that the most common use case for taint APIs involves blocking credentials and secrets from accidentally serializing to client components. Configuration objects often mix safe values (feature flags, public endpoints) with sensitive values (API keys, database URLs). Returning the entire object from a Server Component creates a serialization hazard.

According to recent reports, the standard pattern wraps credential loading with experimental_taintUniqueValue immediately after reading from environment variables or a secrets manager. This marks the value as unsafe before any other code runs. The taint persists for the lifetime of the value, so subsequent function calls and component renders all enforce the restriction.

Attempting to pass the returned object to a client component produces an error at the boundary. React intercepts the serialization and throws before the value reaches the network layer. The error message includes the custom string provided to experimental_taintUniqueValue, making it straightforward to identify which credential leaked and where.

According to recent reports, the pattern extends to authentication tokens and session identifiers. After validating a session and retrieving user data, taint the session token before returning the user object. This prevents accidentally including the token in the serialized response while still allowing safe fields like username and display name to reach the client.

Diagram showing data flow through taint API validation layer.

It has been revealed that the runtime cost of tainting values is negligible. React maintains an internal registry of tainted values using a WeakMap, which does not prevent garbage collection and adds minimal memory overhead. The serialization check happens once per render, not on every access to the value. For applications processing thousands of requests per second, the performance impact remains unmeasurable.

It has been revealed that teams migrating to Server Components often discover existing data exposure issues when they add taint APIs to configuration loading. Code that worked for years suddenly throws errors because it passed internal fields to client components. These errors represent real security holes that authentication and validation layers did not catch. The taint APIs surface the problem before it reaches production.

It has been revealed that authentication and authorization protect resources from unauthorized access. Taint APIs protect values from unauthorized serialization. These concerns overlap but address different failure modes. A Server Action might correctly authenticate a user, verify permissions, and retrieve data: but if the retrieved object contains fields the client should never see, those fields still serialize and reach the browser.

The comparison table highlights where each security layer operates:.

Comparison diagram showing auth checks pass but taint API blocks serialization.

In a recent development, consider a Server Action that loads user preferences. The action authenticates the user, verifies they can access the preferences, and returns the full database row. That row includes safe fields like theme and language, but it also includes internal fields like hashed recovery codes and admin flags. Without taint APIs, all fields serialize to the client because the authorization check passed.

It has been revealed that adding experimental_taintObjectReference to the database row blocks the entire object from serializing. The developer must then explicitly construct a client-safe object containing only the allowed fields. This forces a conscious decision about what crosses the boundary rather than relying on the client to ignore extra fields.

Traditional security patterns operate on request boundaries. Taint APIs operate on serialization boundaries. A single request might cross multiple serialization boundaries as Server Components render, Server Actions execute, and nested client components receive props. Each boundary becomes an opportunity for data leakage if the response includes unintended fields.

According to recent reports, the taint APIs integrate with React's concurrent rendering and streaming architecture. When React suspends a component tree and resumes rendering later, the taint checks remain active. Values marked during the initial render stay tainted when the suspended work completes. This consistency prevents race conditions where a value becomes untainted during suspension.

Recent findings suggest that production implementations typically taint values in two locations: configuration initialization and data access layers. Configuration initialization happens once at application startup, making it the ideal place to taint environment variables and secrets. Data access layers taint database results and API responses before returning them to business logic.

Recent findings suggest that the configuration pattern wraps environment variable access in a typed configuration object that taints sensitive fields during construction. This centralizes the taint logic and ensures every access to the configuration object enforces the restrictions.

Flow diagram showing configuration loading with taint APIs protecting sensitive values.

According to recent reports, the data access pattern taints database rows immediately after retrieval and before passing them to business logic. This prevents any code path from accidentally returning the raw row to a client component. Business logic must explicitly construct response objects containing only allowed fields.

Screenshot showing taint API error message in development tools.

Large codebases benefit from a wrapper module that provides typed configuration access with automatic tainting. The wrapper exports functions that return client-safe subsets of the configuration rather than exposing the raw configuration object. This creates a clear API boundary between server and client code.

Sources indicate that typeScript integration improves the developer experience. Define separate types for server-side configuration (including sensitive fields) and client-side configuration (excluding sensitive fields). The taint APIs enforce this separation at runtime, while TypeScript enforces it at compile time.

In a recent development, the separation between server and client configuration becomes explicit in the codebase. Server Components and Server Actions import getServerConfig, while client components import getClientConfig. The taint APIs enforce this boundary at runtime if any code attempts to pass the wrong configuration type across a component boundary.

It has been revealed that teams adopting taint APIs typically start with high-value targets like authentication tokens and API keys, then expand to configuration objects and database models. The incremental approach allows time to refactor data access patterns and update client components to handle the latest response shapes. For more context on integrating server-side patterns, see extending Electron desktop apps with TypeScript.

Taint APIs prevent values from crossing the server-client serialization boundary managed by React. They do not prevent other forms of data exposure. If server-side code logs a tainted value, that log entry contains the sensitive data. If server-side code sends a tainted value to an external API, that request contains the sensitive data. The taint only blocks React's serialization to client components.

Flow diagram showing taint APIs block client serialization but not logging or external APIs.

The experimental status means breaking changes could occur in future React releases. The API surface and behavior might change before stabilization. Production applications using these APIs should pin React versions and test upgrades carefully. The React team has not committed to a stabilization timeline as of React 19.3.

Recent findings suggest that taint APIs do not protect against client-side vulnerabilities. If client code receives non-tainted data and then exposes it through an XSS vulnerability, the taint APIs provide no protection. If client code stores data in localStorage without encryption, the taint APIs do not prevent that. Client-side security remains a separate concern requiring input sanitization, output encoding, and proper storage handling.

Derived values require careful handling. Hashing a tainted value produces a non-tainted hash, but substring operations on a tainted string produce tainted substrings. The distinction matters for masking operations. To create a masked version of an API key for display (showing only the last four characters), the code must construct a new string rather than slicing the original.

The taint check happens during serialization, not during value creation or assignment. Code can freely manipulate tainted values server-side. The restriction only applies when React attempts to serialize the value and send it to a client component. This means tainted values can safely pass through Server Action boundaries as long as they do not appear in the returned data.

It has been revealed that performance monitoring and error tracking require special consideration. If a tainted value appears in an error stack trace or performance profile, logging that data creates a security risk. Error boundaries and monitoring integrations must sanitize or redact sensitive fields before sending telemetry to external services.

The APIs do not currently support programmatic checks for whether a value is tainted. Code cannot ask React "is this value tainted?" before attempting to use it. The only way to discover a taint violation is to trigger the serialization error. This makes defensive programming difficult, code cannot branch based on taint status.

Sources indicate that react logs an error to the console and prevents the value from serializing, but does not crash the application. The client component receives undefined for that field. In development mode, React throws an error immediately to help identify the issue during testing.

Industry observers note that no, each value can have only one taint message. Calling experimental_taintUniqueValue or experimental_taintObjectReference multiple times on the same value replaces the previous message. The last taint call wins.

Recent findings suggest that yes, as long as the library returns values that React serializes when passing to client components. The taint APIs intercept React's serialization layer, not the data fetching itself. Libraries like tRPC, react-query, or custom fetch wrappers all work with taint APIs when their results pass through Server Component boundaries.

Sources indicate that tainting prevents serialization across React component boundaries at runtime. Encryption protects data during storage and transmission but does not prevent code from passing values to unauthorized locations. Encryption complements taint APIs but serves a different purpose, encrypted data can still leak if passed to client components.

It has been revealed that taint APIs provide runtime enforcement for a boundary that authentication and authorization cannot guard. The boundary between server and client exists at every Server Component render and every Server Action return value. Traditional security patterns check requests and validate inputs, but they do not prevent server-side values from accidentally serializing to client components. The taint APIs close that gap by marking specific values and objects as forbidden, letting React throw an error when serialization would expose them.

Industry observers note that production integration starts with high-value credentials, API keys, database URLs, authentication tokens: and expands to configuration objects and raw database models. The pattern remains consistent: taint the value immediately after loading it, force explicit construction of client-safe responses, and let TypeScript enforce the separation at compile time while React enforces it at runtime. The experimental status requires version pinning and careful upgrade testing, but the protection against accidental data exposure justifies the integration cost for applications handling sensitive data at scale.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes.
  • This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.
  • Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes. Nemotron 3 Content Safety, released in March 2026, combined multimodal and multilingual capabilities for the first time in a single 4B-parameter model. Today, we are releasing Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety, which completes that arc: a single model that unifies multimodal input, multilingual reach, custom enterprise policy enforcement, and auditable reasoning into one inference call.

This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.

Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration. The model takes a user prompt, an optional image, and an optional assistant response as a single context window and produces a coherent safety verdict over the combined input. Evaluating all three together—rather than scoring each independently—closes a well-known gap in multimodal safety scenarios: policy violations that only emerge from the interaction between text and image, or between request and response, are now caught in a single pass.

According to recent reports, nemotron 3.5 maintains the 12-language explicit training coverage of its predecessors—English, French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and Italian—while also inheriting strong zero-shot generalization across approximately 140 languages from the Gemma 3 base model. This means deployments in markets where training data is sparse (e.g., Southeast Asian languages, Scandinavian languages, less-resourced African languages) benefit from base-model multilingual transfer without requiring separate fine-tuning.

It has been revealed that this is the most significant architectural addition in 3.5 relative to Nemotron 3. Production deployments rarely operate under a single universal safety taxonomy. A healthcare platform has a different risk profile than a financial services chatbot, a developer tools IDE, or a children's education app. Nemotron 3.5 accepts a custom policy specification alongside the input. The model reasons over that policy when producing its verdict rather than deferring entirely to the built-in taxonomy. This extends the work first introduced in Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B to the full multimodal, multilingual setting.

In a recent development, every safety verdict in Nemotron 3.5 can be accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace via an optional think mode. When enabled, the model outputs its step-by-step reasoning before delivering a final safe / unsafe label and, optionally, the violated categories.

When latency is the primary constraint, THINK mode can be disabled to return to the same low-latency binary verdict available in Nemotron 3.

In a recent development, with Nemotron 3.5, we are releasing our safety dataset. This is an important milestone since most OSS safety models don't generally provide the training or evaluation sets. This problem is worse for the multimodal space where artifacts such as images or videos are often derived from resources with restrictive licensing terms. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Dataset is multimodal, multilingual, and includes safety reasoning traces that were used to train the model. These reasoning traces were generated in a 2-step manner to make them concise, similar to the Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B model.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT (4B parameters), providing a 128K context window, strong vision-language reasoning, and broad multilingual coverage. NVIDIA fine-tunes this base with a LoRA adapter that installs targeted safety classification behavior while keeping the model compact enough for real-time deployment on 8GB+ VRAM GPUs.

The inference interface supports three output modes:.

Mode 1 — Low-latency binary verdict:.

Mode 2 — Binary verdict with categories:.

Mode 3 — THINK mode (reasoning + verdict):.

The safety taxonomy follows the Aegis 2.0 framework: 13 core categories aligned with the MLCommons safety taxonomy, plus 10 fine-grained subcategories. This alignment allows direct comparison with other open and closed guard systems benchmarked on Aegis-taxonomy datasets.

Reasoning is a supercharger for content safety classification because it provides the necessary context, customization, and accountability required for production AI systems, especially in enterprise and regulated environments.

Enables Custom and Contextual Policy Enforcement.

Reasoning allows a content safety model to dynamically interpret and enforce custom, domain-specific policies defined in natural language at the time of inference. This is necessary because production deployments rarely operate under a single, universal safety taxonomy. A financial services chatbot has a different risk profile than a children's education app which may have a lower tolerance for profanity. This capability supports:.

Provides Auditable and Documented Justification.

The reasoning traces show the model's step-by-step logic before it delivers a final safe or unsafe verdict. This documented justification serves several purposes:.

In a recent development, while reasoning can introduce latency, the Nemotron model addresses this by condensing reasoning chains into concise summaries to limit output tokens and increase efficiency. This is done in a 2-step process similar to what was done in the predecessor model Nemotron-Content-Safety-Reasoning-4B. In the first step, we use larger, more powerful models such as Qwen 397B to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces based upon provided prompts, images, and responses. We also provided the ground-truth labels of the samples to avoid any misclassification that can find its way into the reasoning traces. In step 2, we make these reasoning traces more concise by using another large model such as Qwen 80B. We specifically instruct this model to rephrase the original traces (from step 1) so that it fits in no more than 3 sentences. Based on our experiments, most reasoning traces generated are under 3 sentences.

The efficient reasoning traces optimization allows for low-latency custom policy enforcement. Furthermore, the reasoning traces provide a valuable training signal that can be used for training specialized moderator models. Developers can choose a dual-mode operation, disabling reasoning for minimal latency in generic tasks or enabling it for complex policies.

The dataset driving Nemotron 3.5 is an evolution of the multimodal, multilingual blends used for Nemotron 3, with additions targeting the reasoning and custom-policy capabilities. We have used the following sources of data:.

In a recent development, nemotron 3.5 Content Safety was evaluated across multilingual, multimodal, and custom-policy safety benchmarks, including VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, PolyGuard, RTP-LX, Aya Redteaming, XSafety, MultiJail, Aegis, Dynaguardrail, and CoSA. These evaluations reflect the core production challenge for enterprise safety: applying consistent guardrails across global languages, text and image inputs, and domain-specific policies without adding significant latency.

According to recent reports, nemotron 3 set a strong baseline with 84% average accuracy on multimodal harmful-content tests and roughly half the latency of LlamaGuard-4-12B. Nemotron 3.5 maintains that compact 4B efficiency while adding custom policy support and reasoning traces.

Across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy while maintaining a compact footprint. This matters because many safety models remain English-first, text-only, or too costly to run repeatedly in production pipelines. Nemotron 3.5 is designed to combine multilingual coverage, multimodal classification, custom-policy support, and low-latency deployment in one model.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, averaging about 85% across the evaluated benchmark set.

The language-level results highlight why multilingual safety matters for global enterprise AI. On Multilingual Aegis, Nemotron 3.5 averages 96.5% harmful-content classification accuracy across 12 languages. On RTP-LX, it averages 88.8%, for a combined Aegis and RTP-LX average of 92.7%. This consistency helps teams apply the same safety posture across customer, employee, and partner-facing workflows instead of relying on English-only moderation or separate regional safety models.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 97% harmful-content classification accuracy on Multilingual Aegis Cultural + Adapted (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 89% harmful-content classification accuracy on RTPLX (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Accuracy alone is not enough for production guardrails. Safety models must also be efficient enough to run before content is processed, returned, or routed downstream. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety's compact 4B design helps reduce the cost and latency of repeated safety checks, making multilingual and multimodal guardrails practical for real-world AI applications.

The latency profile is unchanged from Nemotron 3 in the default (no THINK) mode. THINK mode adds inference time proportional to trace length, but this overhead is predictable and can be budgeted separately from the synchronous moderation loop—for instance, by running THINK-mode evaluation asynchronously as part of an audit pipeline while the default mode handles real-time decisions.

Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety achieves 3x lower end-to-end latency on a multimodal benchmark compared to an alternative multimodal safety model.

Compared to another reasoning safety model, our model generated up to 50% fewer tokens when reasoning is enabled, making it efficient in terms of cost and latency.

A recurring theme in multimodal safety research is the gaps in existing evaluation infrastructure. Nemotron 3.5's development encountered the same gaps documented in the broader literature:.

NVIDIA's multimodal training data—with real images and culturally nuanced multilingual prompts—is designed to fill some of these gaps for model training. The benchmark gap for evaluation remains an open problem for the broader safety research community.

In a recent development, nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is available on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License for research and commercial use, along with the training dataset. It supports transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, and is available as a production-grade NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com for teams that need a pre-packaged, GPU-optimized inference microservice.

Developers can also access the model through inference platforms including Baseten, Eigen AI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, and Vultr.

According to recent reports, for custom policy workflows, NVIDIA provides a Claude- and Codex-compatible skill for generating custom policies, along with cookbooks showing how to use the model. Custom policies and reasoning traces help teams adapt safety behavior to domain-specific rules while keeping decisions auditable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For developers and marketers in Thailand and Southeast Asia who maintain landing pages for ChatGPT Ads and want to catch broken tracking before spend begins.
  • OpenAI's Help Center claims UTM parameters on your landing URLs persist on ad clicks, and that ad-review crawlers may visit landing pages with tracking parameters (those visits are not billable clicks).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For developers and marketers in Thailand and Southeast Asia who maintain landing pages for ChatGPT Ads and want to catch broken tracking before spend begins.

OpenAI's Help Center claims UTM parameters on your landing URLs persist on ad clicks, and that ad-review crawlers may visit landing pages with tracking parameters (those visits are not billable clicks). That makes the landing URL itself a piece of infrastructure. If a redirect strips your UTM parameters, your analytics will attribute paid visits to "direct" and you will misjudge the test.

Many sites redirect: http to https, non-www to www, a trailing slash, or a language path such as /th. Some redirect rules drop the query string. The ad click then lands on a clean URL with no UTM.

This script follows redirects and prints each hop plus the final URL, so you can see whether the query string survived.

Industry observers note that this checks the URL path only. It does not prove conversion tracking works, and it cannot tell you whether an ad will be matched. OpenAI states matching depends on conversation context, your landing page, title, copy and context hints, with no delivery guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that our management prepares: THB 30,000 / 50,000 per month in Thailand, US$2,000 / US$3,500 per month elsewhere. Book a free consultation: https://adsgridai.com/contact.

Sources: OpenAI Help Center, Ads in ChatGPT: The Basics; OpenAI, ChatGPT Ads expands to Southeast Asia and Taiwan (23 September 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the organization was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the firm had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the firm’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

It has been revealed that the indictment states the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim manufacturer and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

In a recent development, the government remarked Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

According to recent reports, the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Sources indicate that paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their manufacturer and client data.

Ihme stated RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Recent findings suggest that ihme remarked RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

Sources indicate that A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

Industry observers note that but Ihme stated a review of the firm’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

In a recent development, A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme noted. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

Industry observers note that indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit promptly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

Recent findings suggest that “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a fresh negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

Industry observers note that “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

Ihme noted RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the manufacturer’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

It has been revealed that “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme mentioned. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

Sources indicate that the case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is at the moment facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Recent findings suggest that around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

It has been revealed that in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#57646. What we left out of our MCP server

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1295 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

What we left out of our MCP server

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an MCP server for a database is easy to start and hard to finish.
  • Infino’s MCP server, @infino-ai/mcp-server, gives an agent 15 tools: keyword, semantic, hybrid and SQL retrieval, plus the writes it needs to build and change its own tables.
  • Industry observers note that an agent asks three kinds of questions of the same data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an MCP server for a database is easy to start and hard to finish. The first version wraps a search endpoint and a SQL endpoint. Then the ideas arrive: infer the schema from the first batch, add an upsert, chunk files on the way in, split large uploads and resume them, add a dry run. Each one sounds reasonable, and each one turns the server into a second product with its own bugs.

Infino’s MCP server, @infino-ai/mcp-server, gives an agent 15 tools: keyword, semantic, hybrid and SQL retrieval, plus the writes it needs to build and change its own tables. This post is about the decisions behind that list, most of which were about what not to build, and about what we learned when we handed the server to an agent and watched.

Industry observers note that an agent asks three kinds of questions of the same data. Some need the exact term: an error code, a function name, an order id. Some need the meaning: a question worded differently from the document that answers it. Some need a count, a filter or a join. The usual answer is three systems, a full-text index, a vector store and a SQL database, with a sync job between them.

In Infino all three run on one table, and that table is a Parquet file with its search indexes inside. So the MCP server never routes between backends. infino_keyword_search, infino_semantic_search and infino_hybrid_search rank rows. infino_token_match, infino_exact_match and infino_count filter and tally them. infino_sql reads the same rows with SQL, and the engine’s search functions are callable inside it, so one statement can rank by relevance and then group or join the results. When an agent finds a passage by meaning and then asks how many rows mention the same product, it is reading the same copy of the data both times. We wrote about why that matters in You don’t need two databases for hybrid search.

We set ourselves a rule for the server: expose what the Infino binding does natively, one tool per method, and add nothing of our own. We broke it once.

The engine is bring-your-own-vectors. It stores and searches vectors but does not make them, and an agent cannot produce an embedding by itself. So the server embeds both the documents it writes and the queries it searches, with the same local model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, run through transformers.js). There is no embedding API key to manage, and the text never leaves the machine to be embedded. On Infino Cloud, only the resulting vector reaches the endpoint.

The same reasoning decided who picks the vector dimension. When an agent creates a table with vector: true, the server adds an embedding column sized to its own embedder, with a cosine index. The agent never types a dimension. That number belongs to whoever runs the server, and a wrong guess produces a table whose searches fail later, far from the mistake.

Early versions had a flag, INFINO_MCP_ENABLE_WRITES, and writes were off unless you set it. We removed it in September and did not add a read-only flag in its place. The teams using the server wanted their agents to build and maintain their own tables, and a switch inside the server was the wrong place to say no.

According to recent reports, limits still exist. They live where they belong. On Infino Cloud the API key’s capabilities decide what a connection may do: a read-scoped key is refused every write, and the tool result tells the agent it needs a key with write capability. Every tool also carries MCP annotations, readOnlyHint and destructiveHint, so the client decides when to stop and ask the person at the keyboard. Locally, point the server only at data the agent may change.

The write path is short. Create the table, then append tens of rows per call with infino_add_documents. Each call is one commit, and rows without a vector are embedded together in one batch. To replace rows, delete by key and add them again, and count the matches before any delete.

The list of things we left out is longer than the list of tools.

No schema inference. An agent creates a table from an explicit column descriptor, and a document field that isn’t a column is an error, not a new column. Guessing types from the first batch works until the second batch disagrees.

No upsert emulation. Replacing a row is a delete by key, then an add. Emulating upsert in the server would have meant a read, a diff and two writes that are not atomic together, hidden behind one tool name that suggests they are.

Industry observers note that no splitting, resuming or progress reporting for large uploads. A tool call carries tens of documents, nowhere near the size where a hosted append needs splitting, so that machinery would solve a problem the server cannot have. Loading a whole corpus is a different job, and it already has tools: infino ingest in the Infino CLI, or an SDK.

No file chunking and no dry-run mode. Both are useful. Both belong in the agent or in an ingestion pipeline, not in a thin layer over a database.

Industry observers note that each of these would have been behavior that exists only inside the MCP server, documented nowhere else and tested against nothing else. Keeping the server to the binding’s own surface means there is one implementation of each behavior, in the engine, and the server’s job stays small: describe the tools well, embed text, and pass everything else through.

According to recent reports, some of the most useful changes were small. Semantic search returns a distance, where lower is closer, while keyword and hybrid search return a relevance, where higher is better. An agent comparing scores across tools has no way to know that unless it is told, so every search response says which kind of score it carries, in a score_kind field.

It has been revealed that we also stopped truncating. Earlier versions returned text snippets, which saved tokens but could cut off the part of a passage the agent needed. Hits now return full column values, and the columns argument chooses which fields come back: an id and a line range to cite, the full text, or metadata to filter on. To keep a response small, the agent asks for fewer columns or a smaller k.

Before shipping the write tools, we ran a coding agent headless against the server, allowed to use only the Infino tools, starting cold against a fresh database on Infino Cloud. It worked through four scenarios: ingest a small corpus from nothing, modify and delete rows, answer retrieval questions, and reset the data.

According to recent reports, all four came out correct, in six to ten tool calls each, with no wasted calls. The useful part was where the agent didn’t do what we expected. Asked to find rows containing a literal word, it reached for SQL LIKE and infino_token_match rather than infino_keyword_search. Asked to reset, it deleted every row instead of dropping the table. Neither choice was wrong. Both showed us which tool descriptions weren’t steering it the way we assumed, and for an agent, the tool description is the only documentation it reads.

The server is on npm as @infino-ai/mcp-server and on the official MCP Registry. Setup for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code is in the MCP docs, and the source is on GitHub. To load a whole corpus rather than a few rows, start with the CLI.

It has been revealed that the Infino engine is open source under Apache-2.0. If this post was useful, a star on GitHub helps other engineers find it.

The Open Source Community is backing OpenEnv for Agentic RL

📅 08 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with.
  • Recent findings suggest that starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk.
  • OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with. And today, we’re excited to announce that OpenEnv is becoming even more open, to make the future of training agents open source.

Recent findings suggest that starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk. OpenEnv now lives at huggingface/OpenEnv.

OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.

In a recent development, agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and Hermes just keep improving. One reason for their improvement is that models like GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 are trained to use their respective harnesses.

We want those gains with open source models too: training local models that use harnesses effectively, and saving compute by specializing models for specific tasks.

In a recent development, frontier labs train models and harnesses that, for the most part, work like hand in glove. The model is trained to use the harness and optimised for its characteristics. Models can generalise beyond these harnesses, to some extent, but nothing beats the efficiency of training.

In the open, this isn’t the case. Developers use any harness, any model, any inference engine, on whatever use case they value. This is fundamental to the community, but it’s also a challenge that requires infrastructure and tooling to tackle.

Industry observers note that that’s where OpenEnv comes in. It’s a library to interface between harness, environment, and trainer, which works on any model. For this to stick, it will need to be owned by all the major stakeholders.

Alongside the governance change, we're tightening what OpenEnv is.

In recent releases, OpenEnv has become an interoperability layer for RL environments. Its job is to standardize how environments are published, deployed, and consumed by agents. It will not dictate how rewards are defined or how training loops work. Reward definition, scoring rubrics, and trainer-specific logic belong in the libraries that specialize in them. OpenEnv is the common socket they can all plug into.

In a recent development, one interface, many environments which all expose the familiar Gymnasium-style API (reset(), step(), state()) running on a client/server architecture. A trainer that speaks OpenEnv can drive any compliant environment without bespoke code.

Familiar protocols and canonical packaging. Environments are served over standard protocols like HTTP and WebSocket and packaged with Docker. MCP is a first-class citizen, so OpenEnv environments are instantly compatible with MCP servers and the same environment behaves consistently in both simulation (train/eval) and production modes.

In a recent development, interop across env libraries. You can define and consume environments across different ecosystems (verifiers, harbor, and others) and on the infrastructure and hub of your choice. OpenEnv is the deployment and interface layer underneath them, rather than a competitor to them.

Over the coming months we will focus on the things that turn OpenEnv from a fast-growing project into a dependable standard:.

In a recent development, openEnv is community-centric by design, and it's still early — expect rough edges, and help us smooth them. Check out the code and RFCs: github.com/openenv/OpenEnv.

Thanks to everyone who helped make this transition happen. Let's build the common substrate for open-source agentic RL together.

There is some excellent work here to check. https://a2eprotocol.github.io/docs/.

I typed "Brock Purdy vs Matthew Stafford 2026" into Pigskin Lab, the football stats site I'm building. It reads nflverse play-by-play (data through Nov 19), takes each dropback's change in expected points, averages it per game and per season, and draws the card, the week-by-week trend and the game-by-game bars you see above.

One caveat: this is 9 and 10 games, and EPA is noisy over samples that small, so treat the gap as a lean, not a verdict.

Migrating Your GitHub CI to Hugging Face Jobs

📅 09 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI.
  • That default is convenient, but it also has limits.
  • So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole new test suite that runs on GPU machines!

It has been revealed that in this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:.

That makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

The complete flow looks like this:.

From GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that launches a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

The first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and rolls out HF Jobs in response.

Create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Use cpu-upgrade for real CI so the dispatcher stays available for GitHub webhooks. cpu-basic is fine for testing and will probably work, but it can sleep after inactivity; if GitHub's webhook arrives while it is waking up, the workflow may stay queued forever.

After it builds, open the duplicated Space. You will see a section that says "Required Space secrets," which you can ignore for now. The landing page should display the GitHub App webhook URL you need in the next step. It will look like this:.

If you'd prefer to set up the dispatcher Space with an agent or use a CLI workflow:.

Next, create and install the GitHub App from the dispatcher Space itself. This App needs permission to listen for queued workflow jobs and create ephemeral self-hosted runner registration tokens.

Open your duplicated dispatcher Space:.

In the setup form, enter the GitHub repo whose CI should run on HF Jobs:.

According to recent reports, then click the button to create the GitHub App. GitHub will ask you to choose a name for the App; the name can be anything, as long as it is available in your GitHub account or org. After you submit, the final screen tells you exactly how to upload the App credentials to the dispatcher Space with the hf CLI.

Industry observers note that important note: you will need to provide an Hugging Face token that has permissions to launch Jobs, corresponding to your personal account or an org under which Jobs should be charged. This token should be saved as the HF_TOKEN secret in your dispatcher Space.

In a recent development, finally, you will install the App on the same GitHub repo you entered in the Space. In the Trackio setup, we installed it on gradio-app/trackio.

The GitHub App manifest flow is still browser-based, but an agent can follow the same Space-driven path:.

Paste $GITHUB_REPO into the Space, click the GitHub App creation button, choose any available App name, and follow the generated GitHub instructions.

According to recent reports, after the App exists, install it on your repo from the App settings page. For a GitHub org, the installation settings are under:.

At this point, the dispatcher Space should be configured. The GitHub App setup flow generated the commands that upload the App credentials, webhook secret, and Hugging Face token to the Space.

It has been revealed that by default, HF Jobs are debuted under the same namespace as the dispatcher Space. Optionally, set HF_NAMESPACE as a Space variable if you want to bill jobs to a different Hugging Face user or org:.

The token you set in Step 2 should correspond to this namespace.

use one of the labels handled by the dispatcher:.

For GPU tests, use a GPU label:.

For any GitHub Action you'd like to run on HF Jobs, this 1-line change is all you need!

To add a minimal smoke-test workflow from the CLI:.

You should be able to see logs just like a regular GitHub Action—for example, in this Trackio PR #565.

Note on choosing the right Docker image.

Our first CPU setup used ubuntu:22.04 and installed missing system packages during every run. That worked, but it was slower than it needed to be. GitHub's ubuntu-latest image includes a lot of developer tooling by default; a bare Ubuntu image does not.

In a recent development, for Trackio, the UI tests need Playwright browsers, Node, ffmpeg, sqlite, git, and normal Linux build dependencies. Hugging Face Jobs supports using any Docker image, so we switched to the Microsoft Playwright image, which worked well:.

Here are the numbers from the Trackio CI:.

The biggest win was GPU CI. The Trackio GPU check ran on HF Jobs and passed in 45s, costing less than a cent at the t4-small rate for that duration.

In a recent development, the CPU result was also encouraging. With the right image, the Linux test job was faster than the GitHub-hosted baseline. That suggests HF Jobs can be a practical CI backend, especially for ML projects that need custom images or accelerators.

Logs were another pleasant surprise. GitHub Actions logs are useful, but the web UI can be heavy for large logs. HF Jobs logs are easy to fetch from the CLI:.

Finally, although we didn't need them for Trackio's CI, HF Jobs also supports mounting volumes, which can be very helpful if you need to load datasets or models from Hugging Face quickly as part of your CI.

Hopefully, this gives you all you need to try HF Jobs for running your GitHub Actions!

CreditNirvana Breach Post-Mortem: What Two API Flaws Taught Us About DPDP-Compliant AI Deployment
